summary.executiveSummaryMd: Reduced 64 R4→R6 findings from 57 operation shards. Fresh-review counts: Breaking but probably OK: 25, Revisit: 34, Unclear: 5. 21 reverse-only or purely R6-additive agent findings were moved to non-breaking notable changes.

findings.title: The $apply output return parameter narrows from Any to Resource

changedFields.oldValue: Any
changedFields.newValue: Resource
changedFields.note: The output parameter remains `return` 1..1 and remains the only out parameter; the direct-return resource note appears in both R4 and R6 operation pages.

parameterDeltas.name: return
parameterDeltas.impactMd: The formal output signature no longer permits arbitrary FHIR data types if a validator or generator interprets the OperationDefinition parameter type literally. In practice, both R4 and R6 narrative describe the operation result as a resource returned directly, so non-resource outputs were already inconsistent with the intended operation semantics.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same canonical URL, id, code `apply`, resource `ActivityDefinition`, and type/instance invocation flags. The shard is therefore a direct canonical-url comparison, not a replacement or rename analysis.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The concrete break is for tooling that generated an unconstrained return wrapper from the R4 `Any` type or for conformance tests that accepted `Parameters.return.value[x]` as a valid operation output. The usual runtime path should already consume a direct resource because the R4 operation page says the only `return` out parameter is returned directly as a resource and the R4 comment says the result is a resource of the type specified by the ActivityDefinition.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `ActivityDefinition-apply` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 2. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A test harness generated from the R4 OperationDefinition models `$apply` as returning any FHIR value and includes a negative fixture with `Parameters.parameter[name=return].valueString`. After regenerating from R6, the wrapper expects a `Resource` and the fixture fails validation.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have kept `return.type = Any` and relied on prose, an invariant, or implementation guidance to say only resource results are conformant.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: That would preserve the broad R4 computable signature for generated code, but it would also perpetuate an inaccurate and less useful operation definition. Since the operation pages already describe a direct resource result, tightening the computable type is a proportionate way to improve validation and code generation.

freshReview.rationaleMd: There is a real but narrow codegen/conformance compatibility mechanism. However, the R6 goal is reasonable, the R4 narrative already pointed to resource output, prevalence of intentional non-resource `$apply` returns should be rare, and the less-breaking alternative would keep the formal signature misleading. This does not appear to need renewed standards attention.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The deterministic fanout row for this shard is `r4-only` with match method `unmatched`. The R4 canonical URL is `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CapabilityStatement-conforms`; the R6 package contains no matching file or package-index entry, and no R6 OperationDefinition with code `conforms` scoped to `CapabilityStatement` was found. The R6 `CapabilityStatement-versions` operation remains but serves version discovery, not capability comparison.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a real runtime/API and tooling break: an R4 client or test harness that calls `POST [base]/CapabilityStatement/$conforms`, resolves the R4 canonical OperationDefinition, or generates a typed operation wrapper from the core package will not find a base R6 equivalent. Servers that advertised the core operation in R4 cannot continue to reference a core R6 artifact with the same canonical. The impact is not scored higher because the R4 narrative says full execution was still research-oriented and operation support was optional and likely uncommon.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CapabilityStatement-conforms` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A conformance testing tool generated from R4 core artifacts invokes `POST [base]/CapabilityStatement/$conforms` to compare a client CapabilityStatement with a server CapabilityStatement. Against an R6 ballot4 server and package set, the core operation canonical cannot be resolved and the endpoint is not part of the base operation surface, so the test must fail, skip, or use a custom out-of-band comparison service.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have retained `OperationDefinition/CapabilityStatement-conforms` with the same canonical URL, code, type-level invocation, idempotency/`affectsState: false`, and R4 parameter names while marking the operation `retired`, deprecated in narrative, or explicitly research/optional. The definition could have stated that R6 servers are not expected to support it unless advertised, while still allowing existing clients, validators, and generated code to resolve the canonical artifact.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: The tradeoff is carrying an under-specified comparison operation in core and possibly encouraging continued implementation of semantics the work group no longer wants to advance. That cost appears modest because retaining an optional deprecated OperationDefinition does not require servers to implement it, while removal breaks canonical resolution and typed operation surfaces outright.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The R6 goal of dropping a research-heavy and likely under-implemented conformance-comparison operation is reasonable. However, because the R4 operation was FMM 5 and the same goal could plausibly have been met by retaining a deprecated optional OperationDefinition, the removal deserves renewed design review rather than being treated as an unavoidable break.

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The concrete mechanism is operation-surface removal. A client that knows the R4 route `POST [base]/CapabilityStatement/$conforms` has no base R6 OperationDefinition to discover, validate, or generate against. A server that previously advertised the operation as a core CapabilityStatement type operation has no R6 core canonical artifact to reference. Validators and conformance tests that load core OperationDefinitions will also fail canonical resolution or need a version-specific skip.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Treat `$conforms` as an R4-only core operation unless an R6 server explicitly publishes a custom or IG-defined replacement. Clients should check the server CapabilityStatement for an operation declaration before invoking it and should handle absence as a feature-not-supported condition, not as a failed comparison. Servers that still support the behavior should publish their own OperationDefinition and document whether the R4 parameter names and output shapes are preserved. Cross-version conformance tools should separate the comparison algorithm from the base FHIR operation route so R6 endpoints can be handled by local tooling or explicit implementation-guide contracts.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal appears reasonable: `$conforms` attempted a deep comparison across resources, interactions, search parameters, operations, profiles, value sets, concept maps, and structure maps, and the R4 text acknowledged that full execution was still a matter of research. Even so, a less-breaking base R6 design was plausible. R6 could have retained the canonical OperationDefinition as deprecated, retired, or explicitly optional/research-only while preserving the R4 route and parameter contract for canonical resolution and generated-code stability. That would have avoided hard package and route disappearance without forcing any server to implement the operation. The main downside would be continuing to carry a confusing or under-specified artifact in core.

findings.matchRationaleMd: This is a removal, not a rename or matched change. The R4 operation has id `CapabilityStatement-implements`, canonical URL `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CapabilityStatement-implements`, code `implements`, and resource `CapabilityStatement`. The R6 package contains `OperationDefinition-CapabilityStatement-versions.json` but no `CapabilityStatement-implements` definition and no CapabilityStatement operation with code `implements`; the operation fanout manifest marks the shard `r4-only` and `unmatched`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: For implementations that use `$implements`, the break is hard: the standard route, canonical OperationDefinition, input `Parameters` contract, direct `OperationOutcome` result, and base CapabilityStatement advertisement all disappear. The expected prevalence is probably rare because this operation is specialized conformance tooling rather than a routine clinical exchange API, but generated operation clients, validators, and conformance test suites that include FMM 5 CapabilityStatement operations can fail at runtime or during catalog validation.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CapabilityStatement-implements` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A conformance validation tool generated from R4 invokes `POST [base]/CapabilityStatement/$implements` with `server` and `client` canonical parameters to check whether a server supports a client application. Against an R6-only server or R6-generated SDK, the operation is absent from metadata and the request is rejected or cannot be generated as a standard operation.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have retained `OperationDefinition/CapabilityStatement-implements` as a deprecated or retired trial-use operation while removing it from the base CapabilityStatement advertisement if HL7 no longer wanted baseline server support. The definition could have stated that implementations should prefer explicit conformance tooling or implementation-guide-specific comparison rules, while preserving the canonical URL, code, route, and parameter contract for existing opt-in servers and clients.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: Keeping a deprecated definition would preserve compatibility at the cost of maintaining a weakly specified and probably rarely implemented operation in the core catalog. Removing only the base advertisement would avoid implying broad support while still giving existing systems a standard canonical identity to advertise when they intentionally support it.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The inferred R6 goal of retiring a narrow and limited conformance-comparison operation is reasonable, especially if the operation was under-specified or not widely implemented. But complete removal of an FMM 5 operation creates a direct API and code-generation break, and a modest less-breaking design appears available: retain the OperationDefinition for opt-in compatibility while de-advertising or deprecating it. That combination makes this worth standards/design review rather than treating it as an acceptable cleanup.

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The runtime mechanism is operation identity removal. A request to the standard R4 route `[base]/CapabilityStatement/$implements` or `[base]/CapabilityStatement/[id]/$implements` has no standard R6 OperationDefinition to bind route dispatch, request `Parameters`, output shape, or CapabilityStatement advertisement. findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not assume R6 servers implement `$implements`. During migration, remove standard-operation conformance tests for this endpoint unless the server deliberately provides a local operation. findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 cleanup goal appears reasonable if HL7 wanted to retire a specialized, limited conformance-comparison operation. That design would preserve existing canonical identity, route names, generated code hooks, and opt-in server advertisements. findings.title: The $versions default output parameter gains a required FHIR-version binding

oldOperation.name: Discover what versions a server supports

changedFields.note: The `default` output parameter remains `1..1` code; only its terminology binding changes.

parameterDeltas.name: default
parameterDeltas.impactMd: A validator or generated client that enforces the R6 OperationDefinition can reject or fail to deserialize a `$versions` response whose `default` code is not in the bound FHIR-version value set. R4 did not impose this computable binding, so free-form default labels were not invalid by the R4 OperationDefinition alone.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same id, canonical URL, operation code `versions`, resource association `CapabilityStatement`, and system/type/instance invocation flags. The fanout manifest therefore correctly treats this as a direct canonical-url match, not a replacement or rename.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The operation itself remains callable at `[base]/$versions` with no inputs and the same output names/cardinalities, so ordinary routing and most hand-written clients are unaffected. The concrete break is conformance/tooling: R6 validators, generated clients, or test suites may now treat `default` as a required-bound enum-like FHIR-version code and reject R4-era outputs that used a local label or an official future code absent from the R6 ballot value set. The R6 goal of standardizing default version codes is reasonable, and the R6 code system includes common major.minor and patch values such as `4.0`, `4.0.1`, `5.0`, `6.0`, and `6.0.0-ballot4`, which keeps the practical migration small for servers following the operation prose.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CapabilityStatement-versions` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A multi-version R4 server returns a `$versions` response with `default = "R4"` and `version = ["R4", "R5"]`. That response could pass an R4 OperationDefinition-based Parameters check because `default` was an unconstrained `code`; after regenerating conformance tests from R6, the same response fails the required binding and must be changed to values such as `4.0` and `5.0`.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have used an `extensible` or `preferred` binding on `default`, or a versionless/forward-updatable value set reference, while documenting that official FHIR-version codes are expected.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: Those alternatives would reduce strict-validation failures for local or future labels, but they would not meet the same computable enforcement goal as a required binding. Because the R4/R6 prose already instructs use of major.minor version codes and R6 includes those codes, the stricter design appears proportionate despite some conformance churn.

freshReview.rationaleMd: There is a real old-valid/new-invalid mechanism for R4 outputs that used unconstrained `code` values, and FMM 5/normative status makes the change worth checking. However, the operation's longstanding prose and examples already point to standardized version numbers, the R6 terminology includes the common version forms implementers are expected to use, and the alternative designs would weaken computable validation. This is a small, understandable tightening rather than a change that appears to require renewed standards attention.

evidence.detail: R4 defines the `default` output parameter as required single `code` with no binding.
evidence.quote: {"name":"default","use":"out","min":1,"max":"1","documentation":"The default version for the server. Use the major.minor version like 3.0","type":"code"}

evidence.detail: R6 keeps the same cardinality and type but adds a required binding to the FHIR-version value set.
evidence.quote: {"name":"default","use":"out","min":1,"max":"1","documentation":"The default version for the server. Use the major.minor version like 3.0","type":"code","binding":{"strength":"required","valueSet":"http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/FHIR-version|6.0.0-ballot4"}}

evidence.detail: The R4 operation page renders `default` as `1..1 code` with an empty binding column.
evidence.quote: default ... 1..1 ... code ... [empty Binding] ... The default version for the server. Use the major.minor version like 3.0

evidence.detail: The R6 operation page renders the same output parameter with `FHIRVersion (Required)` in the binding column.
evidence.quote: default ... 1..1 ... code ... FHIRVersion (Required) ... The default version for the server. Use the major.minor version like 3.0

evidence.detail: The R6 FHIR-version code system includes common major.minor, patch, and ballot codes relevant to expected `$versions.default` values.
evidence.quote: Includes codes such as 3.0, 4.0, 4.0.1, 4.3, 5.0, 6.0, and 6.0.0-ballot4.

evidence.detail: The R4 HTTP version-parameter section, referenced by the operation narrative, describes values as publication and major version numbers and shows `fhirVersion=4.0`.
evidence.quote: Accept: application/fhir+json; fhirVersion=4.0 ... The value of this parameter is the publication and major version number for the specification.

evidence.detail: The R6 HTTP version-parameter section likewise describes values as major and minor version numbers and includes examples such as 4.0, 4.3, and 5.0.
evidence.quote: Accept: application/fhir+json; fhirVersion=4.0 ... The value of this parameter is the major and minor version number for the specification.

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The wire-level route and `Parameters` names do not change, but consumers that validate operation results against R6 or generate strongly typed clients from the R6 OperationDefinition may treat `default` as an enum-like FHIR-version code. A legacy R4 server that returned free-form labels can then fail validation, client deserialization, or conformance tests even though the same value was not forbidden by the R4 OperationDefinition.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6 conformance, emit `default` as an official FHIR-version code accepted by `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/FHIR-version|6.0.0-ballot4`. Prefer the major.minor form used by the HTTP `fhirVersion` parameter when that is the endpoint's advertised version, and ensure the `default` value is one of the repeated `version` values. If a server supports a future FHIR version not present in the R6 ballot value set, expect strict R6 validators to need an updated terminology package or local validation policy.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 goal appears to be stronger machine validation and consistent interpretation of the server's default FHIR version. That goal is reasonable because `$versions` exists specifically to support version negotiation, and free-form labels are hard for clients to compare with MIME `fhirVersion` values. A less-breaking base design could have used `preferred` or `extensible` binding, or avoided pinning the value set version, but those approaches would preserve ambiguity and weaken generated validation. Given that R4 prose already directed servers to use major.minor codes and R6's FHIR-version code system includes those common forms, the compatibility break is limited and probably proportionate.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: A less-breaking base R6 design could have kept a deprecated or retired core OperationDefinition for `ChargeItemDefinition-apply`, ideally with an explicit migration note and a pointer to the incubator IG, or retained the ChargeItemDefinition endpoint and `$apply` operation for one transition release while marking both as outside the preferred core workflow.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This is a real operation removal, but the break appears proportionate for core R6: the artifact was very low maturity, R6 ballot narrative gives a coherent goal of moving immature artifacts out of core, and the strongest less-breaking alternatives require retaining deprecated low-maturity resource and operation semantics in the base specification. R4 clients that call `[base]/ChargeItemDefinition/[id]/$apply` cannot find a core R6 OperationDefinition or route generated from the R6 core package. findings.matchRationaleMd: The operation-fanout manifest classifies this shard as `r4-only` and `unmatched`. The R4 operation has canonical URL `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-find-matches` and code `find-matches`; the R6 CodeSystem OperationDefinition files are only `CodeSystem-lookup`, `CodeSystem-validate-code`, and `CodeSystem-subsumes`, and R6 text/package searches found no `find-matches` reference. No likely rename or same-code replacement was identified.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct operation/API break for implementations that used the R4 route or generated code from the R4 OperationDefinition: a client invoking `[base]/CodeSystem/$find-matches` or `[base]/CodeSystem/[id]/$find-matches` against a strict R6 server should not assume the operation exists, and generated R6 client/server stubs and validators will not include the R4 request/response contract. Conformance tests that expected the R4 base CapabilityStatement advertisement also need revision. The prevalence is likely rare because the operation was draft, FMM 0, trial-use, and explicitly preliminary, but the break can be meaningful in terminology transformation workflows that depended on property-based code matching.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CodeSystem-find-matches` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 0. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A terminology transformation service used R4 `$find-matches` with `system=http://snomed.info/sct`, `exact=true`, and repeatable property/subproperty inputs to obtain candidate SNOMED CT codes. After regenerating against the R6 package, the client method and server route are absent, and a conformance test that expects `CapabilityStatement.rest.operation[find-matches]` fails.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have retained `OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-find-matches` with the same canonical URL and R4 parameter schema but marked it `retired`, `draft`, or explicitly legacy/preliminary, and omitted it from the base CapabilityStatement.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: This only partially meets the likely R6 goal. Keeping the artifact in core would continue to expose an unstable, experience-poor operation and might cause generators or conformance tools to keep surfacing a contract the work group no longer wants to encourage. If the goal was to remove an underspecified operation from the base standard rather than merely stop advertising it, full retention would dilute that cleanup.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The change is a real break, but the R4 operation carried the weakest maturity signal and an explicit warning that its interface could change. A less-breaking retired-artifact design was available for tooling continuity, but it has material tradeoffs because it would keep an unstable operation in the core package. Given the low FMM, preliminary text, apparently niche terminology-inferencing use case, and lack of evidence of broad production reliance, the removal looks proportionate rather than a fresh-review `Revisit` case.

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The runtime mechanism is route and contract disappearance. An R4 client can legally call `[base]/CodeSystem/$find-matches` or `[base]/CodeSystem/[id]/$find-matches` with a `Parameters` resource containing required `exact` and repeatable `property` inputs, and parse repeatable `match` outputs. In R6 there is no base OperationDefinition, rendered operation page, operations-list entry, or base CapabilityStatement advertisement for that route, so generated clients may lack a method, generated servers may lack a route, and validators/conformance tests generated from R6 will not know the R4 parameter schema.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Treat `$find-matches` as a legacy/local operation when moving to R6. Servers that still support the R4 behavior should publish an implementation-guide or local OperationDefinition using the R4 canonical or a clearly versioned local canonical and should advertise it explicitly in CapabilityStatement. Clients should use CapabilityStatement feature detection and avoid assuming all R6 terminology servers support this route. Where no legacy operation is available, migration is semantic rather than syntactic: map the workflow to terminology-specific search/mapping services, manual curation, or a local service that preserves the R4 input/output shape.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal is reasonable: remove a draft, FMM 0, preliminary terminology inferencing operation whose own R4 text warned that the interface could change and that may not have gained enough implementation experience. The same goal could have been met only partially with a less-breaking base design: keeping a retired or legacy OperationDefinition in the R6 package while removing it from base CapabilityStatement would preserve canonical/tooling continuity, but would also continue to expose and generate code for an unstable operation. Because the operation is low maturity and explicitly preliminary, the cost of a hard removal is more acceptable than it would be for mature terminology operations such as `$lookup` or `$validate-code`.
