evidence.quote: CodeSystem-lookup ... System Level N/A ... Type Level Yes ... Instance Level No

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: OperationDefinition-driven generators may add an instance-level route and scope `system`/`version` out of that route. Narrative-driven conformance tests may still assert that instance-level support is not part of the terminology service surface. The result is not a removed R4 endpoint, but an R6 route and parameter-scope ambiguity that can produce incompatible clients, server stubs, and tests.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Keep existing type-level `$lookup` behavior. If implementing R6 instance-level lookup, document it explicitly, ensure `code` or `coding` handling is clear when `system` is supplied by the CodeSystem instance context, and avoid treating the R6 terminology-service table as the only source until the ballot conflict is resolved.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal, making instance-level lookup computable, is reasonable because the broader R4 terminology-service narrative already showed `[base]/CodeSystem/loinc/$lookup`. A less-breaking and clearer design would have aligned all R6 normative surfaces and stated whether instance-level support is required or optional. The current mixed signal is more disruptive than either a clean additive route or a clean type-only contract.

findings.title: R6 adds first-class definition and supplement-aware output parts to $lookup responses

changedFields.note: R4 listed `definition` as a standard lookup property but had no top-level out parameter for it; R6 adds one.
R6 lets clients request supplement-aware lookup behavior.
R6 can represent multiple designation use codings.
R6 can identify the supplement that contributed a property.
R6 can identify the supplement that contributed a subproperty.

parameterDeltas.name: definition
parameterDeltas.impactMd: A client that requested `property=definition` in R4 would generally look for it in the generic `property` group because R4 had no named `definition` output. In R6, the matching named out parameter allows servers to return definition as a top-level parameter.

parameterDeltas.name: useSupplement
parameterDeltas.impactMd: This is optional and additive for R4 clients, but R4 servers will not understand it and R6 clients using it need supplement-aware server support.

parameterDeltas.name: additionalUse
parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 responses can convey additional designation use codings that R4 response consumers do not have a defined part for.

parameterDeltas.name: source
parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 responses can identify supplement provenance for a property. R4 clients that enforce the R4 OperationDefinition exactly may reject or drop this part.

parameterDeltas.name: source
parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 responses can identify supplement provenance for a subproperty. R4 clients that enforce the R4 OperationDefinition exactly may reject or drop this part.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The operation is a canonical-url match with the same code and resource context; these are output/input parameter additions within the same operation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Most additions are optional and safe for tolerant `Parameters` parsers. The practical break is for strict R4 output validators and clients that requested `definition` as a generic property and do not look for the new top-level `definition` parameter.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CodeSystem-lookup` is standards-status `normative` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A terminology client requests `property=definition` and has R4-era parsing logic that only scans `Parameters.parameter[name=property].part[code=definition]`; against an R6 server it misses the top-level `parameter[name=definition]`. A strict R4 validator also rejects `property.source` in a response produced using supplements.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have kept `definition` solely in the generic `property` group or required servers to return both the top-level `definition` and a `property` group alias for a transition period. Supplement provenance could alternatively have been represented as a nested subproperty or optional extension.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: Aliases would preserve more R4 client behavior but create duplicate representations and precedence questions. The explicit R6 fields are clearer for new clients and for supplement-aware responses, so the added migration burden appears proportionate.

freshReview.rationaleMd: Less-breaking aliases are possible but carry duplication costs, so this does not appear disproportionate.

evidence.detail: R4 has no `useSupplement`, no top-level output `definition`, no `designation.additionalUse`, and no `property.source` or `property.subproperty.source` parts.
R6 adds `useSupplement` input, `definition` output, `designation.additionalUse`, and `source` parts under property and subproperty.
evidence.quote: "name":"useSupplement","use":"in","min":0,"max":"*","type":"canonical" ... "name":"definition","use":"out","min":0,"max":"1","type":"string"

evidence.detail: R4 operation page lists `definition` in the input property prose but renders no top-level `definition` out parameter.
evidence.quote: The following properties are defined for all code systems: url, name, version ... display, definition, designation, parent and child ... Out Parameters: name, version, display, designation, property...

evidence.detail: R6 operation page renders the new input and output parts.
evidence.quote: useSupplement ... definition ... designation.additionalUse ... property.source ... property.subproperty.source

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: FHIR `Parameters` consumers commonly dispatch by parameter name and nested part name. R6 servers can now produce names and parts that R4-generated parsers did not model. The `definition` addition can also shift a requested property from the generic `property` group to a named top-level parameter.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update `$lookup` clients to read both top-level `definition` and generic `property` entries when consuming concept definitions. Treat unknown output parts as ignorable unless strict validation is required. If using `useSupplement`, expect `property.source` or `property.subproperty.source` and preserve those canonical URLs when staying in R6; drop or extension-map them when converting to R4.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 goal is reasonable: supplements need explicit request and provenance, and definitions are common enough to deserve a named output. A less-breaking base design could have retained only the R4 generic `property` representation or required duplicate aliases, but that would keep response parsing less clear and introduce duplicate same-fact representations. The remaining compatibility risk is manageable with tolerant parsing and dual-read migration logic.

findings.title: R6 drops the explicit allowed subtypes for property.value and property.subproperty.value

changedFields.note: R4 expresses the list using `operationdefinition-allowed-type` extensions; R6 has native `OperationDefinition.parameter.allowedType` but the CodeSystem-lookup artifact does not populate it.
The same constraint loss occurs for nested subproperty values.

parameterDeltas.name: value
parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 generators and validators that rely on the OperationDefinition no longer see the R4 subtype whitelist and may accept, emit, or model arbitrary Element-valued lookup properties.

parameterDeltas.name: value
parameterDeltas.impactMd: The nested decomposition output has the same loss of machine-readable subtype constraints.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The operation is the same canonical `CodeSystem-lookup`; this is a nested output parameter-shape delta within the matched operation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The R4 subtype whitelist is important for generated clients, validators, and conformance tests because `$lookup` property decomposition is explicitly intended for complex terminologies. If R6 is interpreted literally as unconstrained `Element`, R6 servers can produce values that R4 clients and the unchanged CodeSystem.concept.property.value[x] model cannot represent. If the omission is accidental, R6 validators may also under-constrain invalid responses.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CodeSystem-lookup` is standards-status `normative` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A code generator builds an R6 `$lookup` response model where `property.value` can be any Element.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: Populate R6 `OperationDefinition.parameter.allowedType` for `property.value` and `property.subproperty.value` with the same concrete list used in R4: code, Coding, string, integer, boolean, dateTime, and decimal. If R6 intentionally needs more value types, add only those specific types explicitly.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: This would preserve the intended computable contract with little cost because R6 already has a native `allowedType` element. It would also align with the unchanged R6 CodeSystem.concept.property.value[x] type list.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This looks like an avoidable computable-contract regression rather than a deliberate compatibility tradeoff. The change deserves renewed standards review.

evidence.detail: R4 constrains `property.value` with seven `operationdefinition-allowed-type` extensions.
evidence.quote: operationdefinition-allowed-type: code, Coding, string, integer, boolean, dateTime, decimal

evidence.detail: R6 keeps `type: Element` but has no `allowedType` or equivalent extension on `property.value`.
evidence.quote: {"name":"value","use":"out","min":0,"max":"1","documentation":"The value of the property returned","type":"Element"}

evidence.detail: R6 OperationDefinition has a native `allowedType` element for abstract parameter types.
evidence.quote: OperationDefinition.parameter.allowedType ... Allowed sub-type this parameter can have (if type is abstract)

evidence.detail: The underlying R6 CodeSystem property value choice remains the same seven types as R4.
evidence.quote: code, Coding, string, integer, boolean, dateTime, decimal

evidence.detail: R4 rendered page displays the concrete value type union for property and subproperty values.
evidence.quote: property.value ... code | Coding | string | integer | boolean | dateTime | decimal

evidence.detail: R6 rendered page displays only `Element` for both property and subproperty values.
evidence.quote: property.value ... Element ... property.subproperty.value ... Element

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: OperationDefinition-driven validators and generated SDKs use parameter type metadata to decide which `Parameters.parameter.value[x]` names are legal and how to type generated accessors. Removing the allowed subtype list widens the apparent output contract and weakens validation.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Until the R6 artifact is clarified, implement `$lookup` property and subproperty values using the R4/CodeSystem value type set: code, Coding, string, integer, boolean, dateTime, and decimal.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: No evidence in the local R6 CodeSystem StructureDefinition shows a goal to broaden concept property values. If the intended goal was only to move from R4 extension-based allowed types to R6 native `allowedType`, the less-breaking design is straightforward: populate `allowedType` with the existing list. A deliberate broadening to arbitrary Element would be much more breaking and should be justified explicitly because it affects a normative terminology operation.

findings.title: The R6 terminology-server example advertises CodeSystem-lookup under operation name expand

changedFields.note: The R6 base CapabilityStatement still has a system-level operation named `lookup`; the mismatch is in the terminology service example CapabilityStatement.

findings.matchRationaleMd: This compares local core CapabilityStatement advertisements that point to the same CodeSystem-lookup OperationDefinition. The operation itself is the same canonical-url match.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Capability-driven clients and conformance tests discover operations by `CapabilityStatement.rest.operation.name` or `rest.resource.operation.name`. In the R6 terminology service example, the CodeSystem-lookup definition is paired with the wrong name `expand`, so a client looking for `lookup` may conclude the example server lacks lookup or may call the wrong operation. The base CapabilityStatement reduces blast radius because it still advertises `lookup` at system level.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CodeSystem-lookup` is standards-status `normative` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A tutorial or conformance fixture loads the R6 terminology-server example CapabilityStatement and searches CodeSystem operations for `name=lookup`; it fails to find one because the entry is named `expand` even though the definition points to CodeSystem-lookup.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: Keep or add a CodeSystem resource operation entry named `lookup` whose definition is `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-lookup`, and only use `expand` for ValueSet `$expand`.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: There is no meaningful tradeoff; this appears to be a generation or example-authoring error rather than a deliberate design change. Correcting the name preserves capability discovery and aligns with the operation code.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The practical blast radius is limited by the unchanged base CapabilityStatement and by the example status of the terminology-server CapabilityStatement, but the mismatch is concrete, avoidable, and likely to confuse capability-driven tooling. It should be revisited before publication.

evidence.detail: R4 terminology server CapabilityStatement advertises a system-level operation named `lookup` pointing to CodeSystem-lookup.
evidence.quote: system operation: name=lookup, definition=OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-lookup

evidence.detail: R6 terminology-server example advertises the CodeSystem-lookup definition under resource operation name `expand`.
evidence.quote: resource CodeSystem operation: name=expand, definition=http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-lookup

evidence.detail: The R6 base CapabilityStatement still advertises system-level `lookup`, so the issue is not universal across local core CapabilityStatements.
evidence.quote: system operation: name=lookup, definition=http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/codesystem-lookup

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: CapabilityStatement clients often check operation support by matching the advertised operation `name` and then using `definition` for metadata. A mismatched name/definition pair can cause route discovery failures or erroneous operation catalogs even though the OperationDefinition itself remains present.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not infer CodeSystem `$lookup` support solely from the R6 terminology-server example operation names. Capability-driven clients should verify both operation code/name and canonical definition, and server authors should advertise `$lookup` with `name: lookup` wherever they claim support.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: If R6 intended to reorganize terminology operations from system-level to resource-level CapabilityStatement entries, that could be done without renaming the operation to `expand`. The less-breaking design is simply to advertise the same operation code `lookup` with the same definition, optionally at both system and CodeSystem resource levels if both invocation levels are supported. The observed `expand` name does not further a plausible R6 goal for CodeSystem lookup.

findings.title: R6 scopes the system and version inputs to type-level invocation

changedFields.note: R4 OperationDefinition has no parameter scope element; R6 says the `system` parameter applies at type-level invocation.
R4 OperationDefinition has no parameter scope element; R6 says the `version` parameter applies at type-level invocation.

parameterDeltas.name: system

oldValue.documentation: The code system in which subsumption testing is to be performed. This must be provided unless the operation is invoked on a code system instance

newValue.documentation: The code system in which subsumption testing is to be performed. This must be provided unless the operation is invoked on a code system instance

parameterDeltas.impactMd: An R6-aware validator, generated client, or conformance test can treat `system` as not applicable on `[base]/CodeSystem/[id]/$subsumes`. An R4 client that used the same parameter object for both type and instance calls and sent a redundant `system` on an instance call may therefore be rejected or need client-side branching.

parameterDeltas.name: version

oldValue.documentation: The version of the code system, if one was provided in the source data

newValue.documentation: The version of the code system, if one was provided in the source data

parameterDeltas.impactMd: An R6-aware validator, generated client, or conformance test can treat `version` as not applicable on instance-level invocation. This is most likely to affect generic terminology clients that include `version` whenever they know the terminology version, regardless of whether they call the type or instance URL.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same canonical URL, id, operation code `subsumes`, resource `CodeSystem`, and type/instance invocation flags. The shard is a direct canonical-url comparison, not a replacement or rename analysis.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The wire URLs and parameter data types are unchanged, so ordinary type-level calls such as `GET [base]/CodeSystem/$subsumes?system=...&codeA=...&codeB=...` continue to work. The break is narrower: instance-level requests that include `system` or `version` were not computably out-of-scope in R4 but are type-scoped in R6. The R6 goal of making parameter applicability computable is reasonable, especially because `system` is only required when there is no CodeSystem instance in the URL, but strict validators and generated clients may reject previously tolerated redundant parameters.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CodeSystem-subsumes` is standards-status `normative` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A terminology client has one generated `SubsumesParameters` object and calls `/CodeSystem/sct/$subsumes` with `system=http://snomed.info/sct`, `version=...`, `codingA`, and `codingB`. After regenerating from the R6 OperationDefinition, the client wrapper or a server-side validator flags `system` and `version` as not valid for instance-level invocation.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have left `system` and `version` unscoped, or scoped them to both `type` and `instance` while adding prose that they are required only for type-level calls and ignored or checked for consistency on instance-level calls.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: That would preserve more R4-tolerated requests, but it would keep ambiguity about which CodeSystem identity wins when the URL instance, `system`, and `version` disagree. The chosen R6 design gives validators and generators a cleaner contract with a modest migration burden.

freshReview.rationaleMd: There is a concrete runtime/API/codegen compatibility mechanism, but the likely R6 goal is reasonable and the impact is limited to redundant or ambiguous instance-level requests. Because a less-breaking design would preserve ambiguity that parameter scope is designed to remove, this looks like a proportionate tightening rather than a change that clearly needs renewed standards attention.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `system` and `version` as optional inputs without a computable parameter scope.
evidence.quote: {"name":"system","use":"in","min":0,"max":"1","type":"uri"} and {"name":"version","use":"in","min":0,"max":"1","type":"string"}

evidence.detail: R6 keeps the same cardinalities and types but adds `scope: ["type"]` to both `system` and `version`.
evidence.quote: {"name":"system","use":"in","scope":["type"],"min":0,"max":"1","type":"uri"} and {"name":"version","use":"in","scope":["type"],"min":0,"max":"1","type":"string"}

evidence.detail: R6 defines parameter scope as indicating the invocation level where the parameter applies.
evidence.quote: If present, indicates that the parameter applies when the operation is being invoked at the specified level.

evidence.detail: R4 operation narrative supports both type and instance URLs and lists `system` and `version` without a Scope column.
evidence.quote: URL: [base]/CodeSystem/$subsumes ... URL: [base]/CodeSystem/[id]/$subsumes ... system 0..1 uri ... version 0..1 string

evidence.detail: R6 operation narrative renders a Scope column and shows `system` and `version` as type-scoped.
evidence.quote: URL: [base]/CodeSystem/$subsumes ... URL: [base]/CodeSystem/[id]/$subsumes ... system | type | 0..1 | uri ... version | type | 0..1 | string

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: R6-aware tooling can use `OperationDefinition.parameter.scope` to build different parameter sets for type and instance invocation. If it enforces that metadata strictly, instance-level `$subsumes` requests carrying `system` or `version` can fail validation or be impossible to express through generated instance-invocation methods.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6, send `system` and `version` only when invoking `[base]/CodeSystem/$subsumes`. When invoking `[base]/CodeSystem/[id]/$subsumes`, rely on the CodeSystem instance in the URL and send only A/B code or Coding parameters. Servers that want to ease migration can accept redundant instance-level `system` or `version` as a non-fatal consistency check, but conformance tests should align with the R6 scoped parameter contract.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The likely R6 goal is to make applicability of parameters computable: `system` and `version` identify the CodeSystem for type-level invocation, while instance-level invocation already identifies the CodeSystem in the URL. A less-breaking base design could have kept these parameters available at instance level with prose saying they are optional or ignored when redundant. That would preserve more R4 client behavior but would also require conflict rules when the URL instance disagrees with `system` or `version`, weakening the clarity that the new scope field provides.

findings.title: The R6 terminology server CapabilityStatement advertises CodeSystem-subsumes under operation name expand

changedFields.note: The local R4 terminology-server CapabilityStatement advertises terminology operations at the REST level but does not advertise CodeSystem-subsumes. The local R6 example terminology server advertises CodeSystem-subsumes on CodeSystem, but with operation name `expand` rather than `subsumes`.

findings.matchRationaleMd: This finding concerns operation-specific CapabilityStatement advertisement for the same matched canonical OperationDefinition. The OperationDefinition itself still has code `subsumes`, so the CapabilityStatement name is inconsistent with the referenced operation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: CapabilityStatement operation `name` is the name prefixed with `$` and used in the URL. A client, generated SDK, test harness, or documentation page driven by the R6 example terminology CapabilityStatement can conclude that the CodeSystem operation endpoint is `$expand` while its formal definition is `CodeSystem-subsumes`. That can lead to wrong-route invocation or false conformance failures. The blast radius is limited because this is an example terminology server CapabilityStatement in the core package, not a change to the OperationDefinition canonical identity or required support in every server.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CodeSystem-subsumes` is standards-status `normative` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A generated terminology client reads the R6 example terminology server CapabilityStatement, sees a CodeSystem operation with `name` `expand` and definition `CodeSystem-subsumes`, and generates or tests a `CodeSystem/$expand` route for subsumption testing instead of `CodeSystem/$subsumes`.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: Set the CapabilityStatement operation entry to `name: "subsumes"` when `definition` is `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-subsumes`, or omit the advertisement if the example server is not intended to claim support.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: This preserves correct discovery and conformance behavior with no apparent interoperability tradeoff. It is a low-cost correction to an advertisement that otherwise contradicts the OperationDefinition code and operation pages.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This appears to be a direct advertisement inconsistency rather than an intentional R6 design. The less-breaking and more correct design is straightforward, and leaving the mismatch in a core example can mislead generated clients and validators. It should be revisited even though the practical prevalence is limited.

evidence.detail: The local R4 terminology-server CapabilityStatement advertises expand, lookup, validate-code, translate, and closure at the REST level, but does not advertise CodeSystem-subsumes.
evidence.quote: operation names: expand, lookup, validate-code, translate, closure

evidence.detail: The R6 example terminology server advertises a CodeSystem operation named `expand` whose definition is the CodeSystem-subsumes OperationDefinition.
evidence.quote: {"name":"expand","definition":"http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-subsumes"}

evidence.detail: R6 defines CapabilityStatement operation name as the URL operation name and says it should match OperationDefinition.code unless disambiguation is necessary.
evidence.quote: For an operation, this name is prefixed with $ and used in the URL. ... This SHOULD be the same as the OperationDefinition.code of the defining OperationDefinition.

evidence.detail: The R6 OperationDefinition code remains `subsumes`, not `expand`.
evidence.quote: {"code":"subsumes","resource":["CodeSystem"],"system":false,"type":true,"instance":true}

evidence.detail: The R6 operation page shows the actual invocation URLs as `$subsumes`.
evidence.quote: URL: [base]/CodeSystem/$subsumes ... URL: [base]/CodeSystem/[id]/$subsumes

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: Capability-driven tools use `CapabilityStatement.rest.resource.operation.name` to discover the operation segment to call. In the R6 example terminology server, that field points to `$expand` while the definition points to `CodeSystem-subsumes`, so generated clients, dynamic UI forms, or conformance tests can bind the wrong route to the subsumption operation.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not use the R6 example terminology server's `name: expand` entry as the route name for the referenced `CodeSystem-subsumes` definition. Treat the OperationDefinition code and operation page as authoritative for invocation: `[base]/CodeSystem/$subsumes` or `[base]/CodeSystem/[id]/$subsumes`. Conformance artifacts should correct or locally override the advertisement to `name: subsumes`.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The likely R6 goal was to add richer example terminology server CapabilityStatement advertisement for CodeSystem operations. That goal is reasonable and could have been achieved without this mismatch by advertising `name: subsumes` for `CodeSystem-subsumes`. There is no need for a breaking or ambiguous design here; the less-breaking alternative is simply the consistent advertisement.

findings.title: R6 adds optional structured output parameters and SHOULD-level output population guidance

changedFields.note: The existing three output parameters keep the same cardinality and type; R6 adds five optional 0..1 outputs.

changedFields.oldValue: When invoking this operation, a client SHALL provide one (and only one) of the parameters (code+system, coding, or codeableConcept). Other parameters (including version and display) are optional
changedFields.newValue: When invoking this operation, a client SHALL provide one (and only one) of the parameters (code+system, coding, or codeableConcept). Other parameters (including version and display) are optional. When validating a code or a coding, then the code, system and version output parameters SHOULD be populated when possible. When a validating a CodeableConcept, then the codeableConcept output parameter SHOULD be populated when possible.
changedFields.note: R6 adds SHOULD-level conformance expectations for the new structured outputs.

parameterDeltas.name: code

newValue.documentation: The code that was validated

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 responses may include a machine-readable validated code in addition to the R4 `result`, `message`, and `display` outputs. Strict R4 output wrappers that enumerate only the R4 output names may reject or discard it.

parameterDeltas.name: system

newValue.documentation: The system for the code that was validated

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 responses may explicitly return the code system URI. R4-only clients that assumed the system had to be recovered from the request or ignored unknown outputs may lose this normalized value.

parameterDeltas.name: version

newValue.documentation: The version of the system of the code that was validated

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 responses may identify the validated code-system version. Downgrading to the R4 operation shape loses this explicit version result unless an implementation-specific extension or message convention is used.

parameterDeltas.name: codeableConcept

newValue.documentation: A codeableConcept containing codings for all the validated codes

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 can return a normalized CodeableConcept after validating a CodeableConcept input. R4 clients generated from the old OperationDefinition may not model or retain this structured result.

parameterDeltas.name: issues

newValue.documentation: List of itemised issues with paths constrained to simple FHIRPath. Examples are CodeableConcept, CodeableConcept.coding[0], CodeableConcept.coding[1].display, or Coding.display

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 can return itemized validation issues as an OperationOutcome.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same id, canonical URL, operation code `validate-code`, resource `CodeSystem`, and `system=false`, `type=true`, `instance=true` invocation flags. The shard is a direct canonical-url comparison rather than a replacement or rename analysis.

impact.impactRationaleMd: `CodeSystem/$validate-code` is a common terminology workflow and the operation is normative/FMM 5, so even optional output-shape additions matter for generated operation wrappers and conformance tests. The runtime break is limited because the added outputs are optional and the stable R4 outputs remain present, but strict clients or validators that treat the OperationDefinition as a closed output schema can fail on unexpected parameter names.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CodeSystem-validate-code` is standards-status `normative` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A terminology client generated from the R4 OperationDefinition models `$validate-code` output as exactly `result`, optional `message`, and optional `display`. An R6 server returns `result=true`, `display`, `code`, `system`, and `version`; the generated decoder or conformance assertion flags the extra output parameters as unexpected.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have kept the R4 output list unchanged and expressed normalized code/system/version, normalized CodeableConcept, and itemized issues only through the existing `message`, `display`, or implementation-specific extensions.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: That would preserve stricter R4 output wrappers, but it would not meet the same machine-readable terminology goal. Extensions or prose-only conventions would be less discoverable, harder for validators and generated clients to use, and less interoperable than explicit optional OperationDefinition outputs.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This does not appear to need renewed standards attention.

evidence.detail: R4 defines exactly three output parameters: required `result` boolean, optional `message` string, and optional `display` string.
evidence.quote: [{"name":"result","use":"out","min":1,"max":"1","type":"boolean"},{"name":"message","use":"out","min":0,"max":"1","type":"string"},{"name":"display","use":"out","min":0,"max":"1","type":"string"}]

evidence.detail: R6 keeps the R4 outputs and adds optional `code`, `system`, `version`, `codeableConcept`, and `issues` outputs.
evidence.quote: {"name":"issues","use":"out","min":0,"max":"1","documentation":"List of itemised issues with paths constrained to simple FHIRPath. Examples are CodeableConcept, CodeableConcept.coding[0], CodeableConcept.coding[1].display, or Coding.display","type":"OperationOutcome"}

evidence.detail: The R4 operation page output table shows only `result`, `message`, and `display`.
evidence.quote: Out Parameters: result 1..1 boolean; message 0..1 string; display 0..1 string

evidence.detail: The R6 operation page adds SHOULD-level output population guidance and renders the new structured outputs.
evidence.quote: When validating a code or a coding, then the code, system and version output parameters SHOULD be populated when possible. When a validating a CodeableConcept, then the codeableConcept output parameter SHOULD be populated when possible. ... code ... system ... version ... codeableConcept ... issues

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The operation response is a `Parameters` resource whose named parts are commonly turned into generated method return models or conformance fixtures. R6 servers may include new optional output parts that were not in the R4 OperationDefinition. Robust clients should ignore or preserve unknown `Parameters.parameter` entries, but strict R4-generated wrappers, validators, or golden-file tests may reject a response containing `code`, `system`, `version`, `codeableConcept`, or `issues`.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Regenerate `$validate-code` clients and server stubs from the R6 OperationDefinition, and make decoders tolerant of additional output parameters while continuing to require `result`. Servers should keep populating `result`, use `message` and `display` as before, and add `code`, `system`, `version`, `codeableConcept`, and `issues` when available. R4 bridge layers should either drop the added outputs explicitly with documented loss or map them to local extensions outside the base R4 operation contract.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal is to make validation responses more machine-readable: a client can learn exactly which code/system/version was validated, receive a normalized CodeableConcept, and inspect itemized issues instead of parsing free text. That goal is reasonable for a mature terminology operation. A less-breaking base design could have kept the R4 output shape and used only `message`, `display`, or extensions, but that would be substantially less interoperable and would not give generated code or validators a standard contract for the added details. Because the additions are optional and do not remove the R4 outputs, the compatibility cost is real but proportionate.

findings.title: R6 example terminology CapabilityStatement advertises CodeSystem-validate-code with operation name expand

changedFields.oldValue: The local R4 terminology-server CapabilityStatement has no CodeSystem resource operation entry for CodeSystem-validate-code.
changedFields.note: The R6 example terminology server adds a CodeSystem resource-level advertisement, but the operation name does not match the OperationDefinition code `validate-code`.

findings.matchRationaleMd: This finding concerns CapabilityStatement advertisement for the same canonical OperationDefinition matched in this shard. It is not a separate operation replacement: the referenced OperationDefinition is still `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-validate-code`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The primary risk is capability-driven tooling rather than the wire contract of the OperationDefinition itself. A client or test generator that trusts the R6 example terminology CapabilityStatement can associate the validate-code definition with `$expand`, miss the advertised `$validate-code` support, or produce inconsistent conformance expectations. The entry also carries a SHALL expectation extension, increasing the conformance significance of the mismatch.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `CodeSystem-validate-code` is standards-status `normative` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A conformance test generator reads the R6 example terminology server CapabilityStatement and creates a CodeSystem `$expand` test whose expected definition is CodeSystem `$validate-code`, while omitting a correct CodeSystem `$validate-code` route from the generated server capability model.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: Advertise the CodeSystem operation with `name: "validate-code"` when the definition is `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-validate-code`; keep any separate `$expand` advertisement tied only to an OperationDefinition whose code is `expand`.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: This is a low-cost correction with no apparent loss of R6 functionality. It preserves capability-driven discovery while still allowing the example terminology server to advertise CodeSystem operations.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The mismatch appears avoidable and directly affects machine-readable conformance metadata for a common normative operation. Because a simple base artifact correction can meet the apparent R6 goal with no meaningful tradeoff, this should be revisited rather than treated as proportionate breakage.

evidence.detail: The R6 example terminology server has a CodeSystem resource operation with `name` `expand`, definition `CodeSystem-validate-code`, and a SHALL expectation extension.
evidence.quote: {"extension":[{"url":"http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/capabilitystatement-expectation","valueCode":"SHALL"}],"name":"expand","definition":"http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-validate-code"}

evidence.detail: The OperationDefinition code remains `validate-code`, so the CapabilityStatement operation name should not be `expand` for this definition.
evidence.quote: "code":"validate-code","resource":["CodeSystem"],"system":false,"type":true,"instance":true

evidence.detail: The R4 terminology-server CapabilityStatement did not contain CodeSystem resource operation entries, while the R6 example terminology server did; the R4 and R6 base CapabilityStatements both retain legacy system-level `validate-code` entries and therefore are not the source of this specific resource-level name mismatch.

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: CapabilityStatement-driven clients and test tools use `operation.name` to discover the `$name` URL segment and `operation.definition` to attach the formal OperationDefinition contract. In the R6 example terminology server entry, these two fields disagree: the URL segment implied by `name` is `$expand`, while the formal contract is CodeSystem `$validate-code`. That can create wrong generated routes, missing `$validate-code` capability assertions, or false conformance failures.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not copy the R6 example terminology server CodeSystem operation names without checking that each name matches its OperationDefinition code. Advertise CodeSystem `$validate-code` with operation `name` `validate-code` and definition `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/CodeSystem-validate-code`. CapabilityStatement consumers should prefer reconciling `name` and `definition.code` and flag mismatches rather than silently generating routes from one field alone.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The apparent R6 goal is to advertise CodeSystem terminology operations more explicitly in the example terminology server CapabilityStatement. That goal is reasonable, but the name/definition mismatch is not necessary to achieve it. A less-breaking and more correct base design is simply to use the matching operation name `validate-code`; this preserves discovery and conformance semantics without introducing ambiguity for generated clients or validators.

findings.title: R6 removes the R4 type-level $document invocation and id parameter

changedFields.note: R4 allowed type-level invocation on `Composition`; R6 limits the operation to instances.
The R4 operation page lists both URLs and says the instance GET is identical in meaning to the type-level GET with `id`; the R6 operation page lists only the instance URL.

parameterDeltas.name: id

oldValue.documentation: Identifies the composition to use. This can either be a simple id, which identifies a composition, or it can be a full URL, which identifies a composition on another server.

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 clients could supply `id` to `GET [base]/Composition/$document?id=[id]` or in a POSTed Parameters body. R6-generated clients and validators no longer expose or accept that parameter, and R6 servers following the base OperationDefinition need only route `[base]/Composition/[id]/$document`.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same canonical URL, id, operation code `document`, and resource context `Composition`, so this is a direct canonical-url comparison rather than a replacement or rename analysis.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a concrete operation-route and parameter-contract break. R4 clients that used the documented type-level route, especially POST with a Parameters body containing `id`, may receive 404/400 from an R6 server or fail generated-client compilation because the `id` input is gone. R4 servers that advertised and tested both type and instance forms will fail R6 conformance if they continue to claim the removed base route. The R6 goal appears to be simplifying `$document` around an identified Composition instance and avoiding two ways to locate the target resource, which is reasonable, but the same goal could have been met with a less-breaking transitional base design.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Composition-document` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 2. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A document-generation client built from the R4 example sends `POST [base]/Composition/$document` with `Parameters.parameter[name=id].valueUri` and `persist=true`. After a server upgrades to R6 and implements only the base R6 instance route, the request no longer matches the operation contract.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have kept `type: true` and retained the optional `id` parameter, while marking the type-level form as deprecated or secondary and stating that `[base]/Composition/[id]/$document` is preferred. The `id` parameter could still be prohibited when the operation is invoked on an instance, preserving the R4 ambiguity guard.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: The tradeoff is continued support for two equivalent URL shapes and some server/codegen surface area. That burden is modest compared with removing a documented R4 invocation path, and it would not prevent R6 from recommending the clearer instance-level design.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The break is direct, visible at runtime, and avoidable with a low-cost compatibility design. Because the R6 operation is normative and document generation is a central Composition use case, this change deserves renewed design review unless there is an unstated safety or interoperability reason to forbid type-level invocation.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `$document` on Composition with `type: true`, `instance: true`, and an optional `id` input parameter.
evidence.quote: "resource":["Composition"],"system":false,"type":true,"instance":true,"parameter":[{"name":"id","use":"in","min":0,"max":"1","documentation":"Identifies the composition to use...","type":"uri"}, ...]

evidence.detail: R6 defines `$document` on Composition with `type: false`, `instance: true`, and no `id` input parameter.
evidence.quote: "resource":["Composition"],"system":false,"type":false,"instance":true,"parameter":[{"name":"persist",...},{"name":"graph",...},{"name":"return",...}]

evidence.detail: The R4 operation page lists both type and instance URLs and documents the equivalence and restrictions for the `id` parameter.
evidence.quote: URL: [base]/Composition/$document ... URL: [base]/Composition/[id]/$document ... GET [base]/Composition/[id]/$document is identical in meaning to GET [base]/Composition/$document?id=[id]

evidence.detail: The R6 operation page lists only the instance URL and renders only `persist` and `graph` as input parameters.
evidence.quote: URL: [base]/Composition/[id]/$document ... In Parameters: ... persist ... graph

evidence.detail: The R4 example explicitly demonstrates the type-level POST form with an `id` parameter in the Parameters body.
evidence.quote: POST http://fhir.healthintersections.com.au/open/Composition/$document ... <name value="id"/> ... <valueUri value="180f219f-97a8-486d-99d9-ed631fe4fc57"/>

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The wire operation endpoint changes from accepting a resource-type operation with an identifying parameter to accepting only an instance operation. This affects HTTP routing, generated operation client methods, server dispatch tables, parameter validation, and conformance tests that assert the R4 equivalence between `Composition/$document?id=...` and `Composition/[id]/$document`.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Prefer the R6 instance route: `GET [base]/Composition/[id]/$document` or `POST [base]/Composition/[id]/$document` with only `persist` and/or `graph` in Parameters. R6 servers with R4 clients should consider retaining `Composition/$document` plus `id` as an explicitly documented compatibility extension, while not advertising it as the base R6 OperationDefinition unless local conformance policy allows extensions.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal of eliminating a duplicate target-identification mechanism is understandable: the operation is semantically about generating a document from a specific Composition. However, R4 explicitly specified the type-level form and used it in the POST example. A less-breaking base design could have retained the old `type` invocation and optional `id` input as deprecated while recommending instance invocation. That would preserve most R4 clients and tests at moderate implementation cost, so the base R6 removal appears probably avoidable.

findings.title: R6 formalizes a direct Bundle return where R4 had no out parameter and search-wrapper prose

changedFields.note: R6 adds a required out parameter that, because it is the sole resource out parameter named `return`, is returned directly as the operation response resource.

changedFields.oldValue: R4 description includes: "Note that since this is a search operation, the document bundle is wrapped inside the search bundle."
changedFields.newValue: R6 description removes the search-operation/search-bundle wrapper sentence.
changedFields.note: The R4 operation page nevertheless shows a direct document Bundle example, so the practical R4 behavior is ambiguous.

parameterDeltas.name: return

newValue.documentation: The bundle containing the composition and resources associated with it.

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 code generators and validators can now require a direct `Bundle` result for this operation. R4 tooling generated from the computable OperationDefinition had no declared output parameter, while clients following the R4 description could have expected a searchset Bundle wrapper containing the document Bundle.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The operation identity is unchanged by canonical URL and code; this finding isolates the changed output contract and operation-specific narrative for the same `$document` operation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: A literal R4 implementation could return or expect a searchset wrapper because the R4 description says the document bundle is wrapped inside a search bundle. Such clients and servers would not interoperate cleanly with the R6 direct-return contract and may fail conformance tests that assert the sole `return` parameter is a direct Bundle. The R6 goal is reasonable because the operation is to generate a FHIR document Bundle and the R4 example already showed a direct document Bundle response, but the R4 text conflict makes real-world prevalence uncertain.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Composition-document` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 2. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: An R4 server implemented the text literally and returns `Bundle.type=searchset` whose first entry is a document `Bundle`. An R6 client generated from the new OperationDefinition expects the response resource itself to be the document Bundle and fails when it sees a searchset wrapper.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have added the `return` Bundle parameter while explicitly allowing a transitional R4-compatible searchset wrapper, or could have profiled/documented both accepted response shapes with a preference for direct document Bundle.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: That would preserve clients that followed the R4 wrapper prose, but it would also perpetuate a two-shape response contract for a normative operation and make clients, validators, and tests handle both direct and wrapped Bundle results. If the R4 wrapper sentence was simply erroneous, retaining it would weaken the cleanup.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The response-shape change may be breaking, but R4 evidence conflicts: the computable R4 OperationDefinition has no out parameter, the R4 description says search wrapper, and the R4 example returns a direct document Bundle. Because prevalence and intended semantics are uncertain, this should be reviewed by a human rather than classified as clearly acceptable or clearly avoidable.

evidence.detail: R4 has only input parameters `id`, `persist`, and `graph`; it declares no output parameter.
evidence.quote: "parameter":[{"name":"id","use":"in",...},{"name":"persist","use":"in",...},{"name":"graph","use":"in",...}]

evidence.detail: R4 description says the document bundle is wrapped inside a search bundle.
evidence.quote: Note that since this is a search operation, the document bundle is  wrapped inside the search bundle.

evidence.detail: R6 declares a required output parameter named `return` of type `Bundle`.
evidence.quote: {"name":"return","use":"out","min":1,"max":"1","documentation":"The bundle containing the composition and resources associated with it...","type":"Bundle"}

evidence.detail: The R6 operation page renders the required out parameter and states that it is returned directly as a resource.
evidence.quote: Out Parameters: ... return ... 1..1 ... Bundle ... Note: as this is the only out parameter, it is a resource, and it has the name 'return', the result of this operation is returned directly as a resource

evidence.detail: The R4 example response starts with a direct Bundle whose `type` is `document`, not an obvious searchset wrapper.
evidence.quote: Response: ... <Bundle> ... <type value="document"/>

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The operation result can be interpreted differently by clients and servers: R6 has a formal direct `Bundle` return, while R4 prose permitted or implied a search operation response wrapper.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: R6 clients should treat the HTTP response body as the generated document `Bundle` itself. R4 servers that returned a searchset wrapper should either update the R6 endpoint to return the document Bundle directly or clearly document a compatibility endpoint/extension for older clients. Test suites should avoid assuming R4 wrapper behavior unless they are explicitly testing an R4 endpoint that chose that interpretation.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal is to make the operation result computable and consistent with FHIR document semantics. That is reasonable and likely improves generated code and validators. A less-breaking design could have kept both direct and wrapped response shapes during transition, but this would preserve ambiguous normative behavior and force every client to support two Bundle interpretations. Because R4 evidence is contradictory, the need for a less-breaking base design is plausible but not proven.

findings.title: R6 core removes the ConceptMap $closure operation

changedFields.note: No R6 core OperationDefinition with this canonical URL, id, operation code, or closure-table purpose was found.

changedFields.oldValue: closure
changedFields.note: The executable `$closure` route segment disappears from the R6 core operation set.
The R4 operation is associated with ConceptMap; R6 core has no corresponding ConceptMap closure operation.

oldValue.narrativeCaveat: The detailed R4 terminology-service examples use [base]/ConceptMap/$closure, but the computable OperationDefinition and primary operation page define system-level invocation.

changedFields.note: R4 defines a system-level closure-table operation. R6 core removes the route by removing the OperationDefinition.

oldValue.operationPageText: This is not an idempotent operation
oldValue.statefulSemantics: The server tracks closure-table context names and response versions for replay/resynchronization.

changedFields.note: R4 does not carry a computable `affectsState` element in this artifact, but its rendered page and terminology-service narrative describe non-idempotent, stateful behavior. R6 core has no statefulness declaration because the operation is absent.

changedFields.oldValue: name 1..1 string; concept 0..* Coding; version 0..1 string.
changedFields.note: All input parameters are removed with the operation. The required R4 `name` context and version replay contract have no R6 core counterpart.

changedFields.oldValue: return 1..1 ConceptMap, direct resource return because it is the only output parameter and is named `return`.
changedFields.note: The required direct ConceptMap response carrying closure-table delta entries is removed with the operation.

changedFields.oldValue: R4 parameters have no bindings, profiles, or nested parts.
changedFields.note: The material change is operation removal, not a binding, profile, or part-shape tightening.

changedFields.oldValue: R4 describes initializing a named closure table, adding one or more Coding values, returning ConceptMap deltas, version replay/resynchronization, error cases, and client use of the table for terminology-aware search.
changedFields.note: R6 has no closure operation page and the R6 terminology-service page has no closure-table section.

changedFields.newValue: No R6 core CapabilityStatement closure operation advertisement found.
changedFields.note: R4 base and terminology-server CapabilityStatements advertise closure; R6 core CapabilityStatements do not.

changedFields.oldValue: R4 operations list includes `Closure Table Maintenance` at `[base]/$closure`.
changedFields.newValue: R6 operations list includes ConceptMap `$translate` but no `$closure` entry.
changedFields.note: The rendered operation-list surface agrees with the package-level removal.

parameterDeltas.name: name

oldValue.documentation: The name that defines the particular context for the subsumption based closure table

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 callers were required to supply a named closure-table context. R6 core has no corresponding required input, so generated request builders and validators cannot map an R4 initialization, add, or resynchronization request to a core R6 operation contract.

parameterDeltas.name: concept

oldValue.documentation: Concepts to add to the closure table

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 clients could submit zero or more Coding values to initialize or update the closure table. R6 core has no operation-specific input for adding concepts to a client-maintained closure table.

parameterDeltas.name: version

oldValue.documentation: A request to resynchronise - request to send all new entries since the nominated version was sent by the server

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 clients could ask the server to replay closure-table changes since a prior response version. R6 core removes that replay contract, so restart/recovery workflows need a local or IG-specific synchronization design.

parameterDeltas.name: return

oldValue.documentation: A list of new entries (code / system --> code/system) that the client should add to its closure table. The only kind of entry mapping equivalences that can be returned are equal, specializes, subsumes and unmatched

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 clients expected a direct ConceptMap resource containing closure-table delta mappings.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The operation-fanout row marks `ConceptMap-closure` as `r4-only` with match method `unmatched`. The R4 package contains `OperationDefinition-ConceptMap-closure.json`; the R6 package has no `OperationDefinition-*closure*.json` and no OperationDefinition content matching `ConceptMap-closure`, `$closure`, or closure-table terminology. R6 candidate operation pages are 404 and the R6 operations list has no closure entry.

impact.impactRationaleMd: For implementations that used R4 closure-table maintenance, this is a hard runtime and API break: the base canonical OperationDefinition, route, request parameters, direct ConceptMap response, version replay semantics, and CapabilityStatement advertisement disappear. The expected prevalence is not universal because `$closure` is a specialized terminology optimization, but R4 documented it as solving an important terminology/search use case and advertised it as SHOULD for terminology servers. The inferred R6 goal of avoiding a stateful, specialized synchronization protocol in core is reasonable, yet deleting the OperationDefinition entirely is more disruptive than lowering conformance expectations or deprecating a retained legacy contract.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `ConceptMap-closure` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 3. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: An R4 terminology client maintains a local SNOMED CT closure table for clinical search. On startup it calls `$closure` with `name` and `version` to recover missed deltas, then sends new `concept` Coding values as they appear. Against an R6-core-generated terminology server there is no base `$closure` route or OperationDefinition, so the generated client call and conformance test fail and the application must redesign how it keeps terminology-aware search indexes current.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 core could have retained `OperationDefinition/ConceptMap-closure` as a legacy/deprecated trial-use operation with the same operation code and input names, removed or downgraded the terminology-server SHOULD advertisement to MAY, and added narrative that new implementations should prefer other terminology strategies unless they explicitly need closure-table synchronization.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: This would preserve the canonical contract and generated-code surface for existing users while still signaling reduced strategic importance. The tradeoff is that R6 core would continue carrying a stateful, specialized, apparently low-adoption operation and would need to describe how its ConceptMap return maps to the R6 ConceptMap model.

freshReview.rationaleMd: Because the operation is removed rather than merely deprecated, real R4 clients and servers lose a route-level API and conformance target. The R6 goal appears plausible, but the supplied evidence does not show why a retained legacy optional OperationDefinition would fail that goal. Given FMM 3/trial-use maturity, terminology-server SHOULD advertisement, and a plausible lower-cost compatibility design, this deserves renewed review.

evidence.detail: R4 computable OperationDefinition defines canonical identity, code `closure`, resource `ConceptMap`, system-level invocation, and four parameters.

Primary R4 operation page describes purpose, URL, non-idempotence, parameter table, and direct ConceptMap return.

FMM/status context for ConceptMap-closure.

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: A client or generated SDK that calls the R4 core `$closure` operation will not find a base R6 OperationDefinition, route template, parameter validator, or response schema. A server generated from R6 core definitions will not expose or advertise `$closure` unless it carries a custom legacy definition. Conformance suites comparing core CapabilityStatement operations will also see R4 `closure` advertisements disappear in R6.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Servers that need continuity should publish a local or IG-defined legacy `$closure` OperationDefinition, explicitly advertise it in CapabilityStatement, and document whether they accept the R4 system-level `[base]/$closure` route, the R4 terminology-page `[base]/ConceptMap/$closure` examples, or both. Clients should feature-detect the operation before use and provide fallback behavior, such as rebuilding local closure tables from terminology-specific exports, using precomputed subsumption indexes, issuing `$subsumes` checks, or adapting search logic around value-set expansion where clinically safe.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The breaking effect is avoidable in part because the R6 goal could likely be met by lowering the core expectation rather than deleting the canonical operation. Keeping `ConceptMap-closure` as deprecated/legacy and optional would preserve the R4 route and parameter names for implementers that already use it while signaling that the stateful protocol is no longer a preferred core terminology feature. The tradeoff is ongoing core-spec clutter and the need to define its R6 ConceptMap return semantics, but that appears less disruptive than removing an FMM 3 operation that R4 terminology-server conformance advertised as SHOULD.

findings.title: R6 renames the $translate input surface and replaces reverse with source/target inputs

changedFields.note: R6 source-prefixes the old concept selector parameters. Only `sourceSystem` and `sourceVersion` documentation says servers MAY still accept the previous names `system` and `version`; the formal R6 OperationDefinition does not define old `code`, `coding`, or `codeableConcept` aliases.

R6 removes the R4 `reverse` flag and instead lets clients identify a target concept directly with `targetCode`, `targetCoding`, or `targetCodeableConcept`. The old `source` and `target` value-set parameters are renamed to `sourceScope` and `targetScope`.
The input dependency part is renamed and widened from a CodeableConcept-only value to a generic Element value.

changedFields.oldValue: One and only one of code, coding, or codeableConcept must be provided.
changedFields.newValue: One and only one of sourceCode, sourceCoding, sourceCodeableConcept, targetCode, targetCoding, or targetCodeableConcept SHALL be provided.
changedFields.note: The operation can now be asked from either source-side or target-side concept identity, rather than using R4's `reverse` boolean.

parameterDeltas.name: code/sourceCode
parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 requests and generated method signatures using `code` no longer match the formal R6 input name. If a strict R6 server ignores unknown parameters, a request with `code` may fail the R6 one-of-source-or-target input rule because `sourceCode` is absent.

parameterDeltas.name: system/sourceSystem

newValue.name: sourceSystem
newValue.documentation: The previous name of this input parameter was `system`, and servers MAY choose to still accept that name.

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 gives a MAY-level compatibility note for `system`, but it is not a formal alias. Clients cannot depend on every R6 server accepting the R4 name.

parameterDeltas.name: version/sourceVersion

newValue.name: sourceVersion
newValue.documentation: The previous name of this input parameter was `version`, and servers MAY choose to still accept that name.

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 gives only optional server compatibility for the old `version` name. Strict clients and conformance tests should use `sourceVersion`.

parameterDeltas.name: coding/sourceCoding
parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 clients that POST a `Parameters` resource with an input part named `coding` must rename it to `sourceCoding` for a formally conformant R6 request.

parameterDeltas.name: codeableConcept/sourceCodeableConcept
parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 request bodies using `codeableConcept` do not satisfy the formal R6 parameter name and need an explicit rename.

parameterDeltas.name: source/sourceScope
parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 examples and clients that pass `source` to constrain the source value set need to use `sourceScope` in R6.

parameterDeltas.name: target/targetScope and targetsystem/targetSystem
parameterDeltas.impactMd: The target value-set parameter is renamed, and the target code-system parameter changes capitalization from `targetsystem` to `targetSystem`. Query builders and case-sensitive `Parameters` parsers must update both names.

parameterDeltas.name: targetCode/targetCoding/targetCodeableConcept
parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 uses explicit target concept inputs for target-to-source translation. This is more expressive than R4 `reverse=true`, but R4 clients must transform the old reverse request shape rather than just rename one parameter.

parameterDeltas.name: reverse
parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 clients that set `reverse=true` need to express the lookup using R6 target-side inputs. There is no formal R6 `reverse` parameter for a server to accept.

parameterDeltas.name: dependency
parameterDeltas.impactMd: Dependency parameters must be renamed and can carry a broader Element value in R6. R4 servers or clients expecting `dependency.concept` as a CodeableConcept will not parse the R6 dependency shape without custom mapping.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same id, canonical URL, operation code `translate`, resource `ConceptMap`, and `system=false`, `type=true`, `instance=true` invocation flags. The shard is a direct canonical-url comparison, so these parameter differences are changes to the same operation rather than a replacement operation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct runtime and generated-code break for clients that use the R4 `$translate` request parameter names shown in the R4 examples. A strict R6 server is not required to accept `code`, `coding`, `codeableConcept`, `source`, `target`, `targetsystem`, `reverse`, or `dependency.element/concept`; even the compatibility notes for old `system` and `version` are MAY-level and incomplete without an old `code` alias.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `ConceptMap-translate` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 3. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A terminology client generated from the R4 OperationDefinition invokes `GET [base]/ConceptMap/$translate?system=http://hl7.org/fhir/composition-status&code=preliminary&source=http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/composition-status&target=http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/v3-ActStatus`. A strict R6 server expects `sourceSystem`, `sourceCode`, `sourceScope`, and `targetScope`; it ignores or rejects the old names and reports that the required source/target concept choice was not supplied.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have kept the old input parameter names as formal deprecated aliases while adding the clearer `source*` and `target*` names. For example, `code`, `coding`, and `codeableConcept` could be documented as aliases for the corresponding `source*` inputs; `source` and `target` as aliases for `sourceScope` and `targetScope`; `targetsystem` as an alias for `targetSystem`; and `reverse=true` as a deprecated way to indicate target-to-source lookup when only the R4 source-side concept inputs are supplied.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: The tradeoff is a larger operation contract with duplicate ways to express the same request and precedence rules when old and new names are mixed. That cost is real, but the R6 text already introduces MAY-level aliases for `system` and `version`, so a more complete alias/deprecation design appears feasible and would preserve most R4 requests while still allowing the clearer R6 model.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The R6 goal is reasonable: make source and target directions explicit and align request parameters with the R6 ConceptMap relationship model. The specific base design still deserves renewed attention because common R4 request shapes stop being formal R6 requests, the R6 compatibility notes cover only two old names, and a low-cost alias/deprecation path could have carried most R4 clients through the transition.
