evidence.detail: The package parameter names are `measureUrl`, `periodStart`, `periodEnd`, `subject`, `subjectGroup`, `reporter`, `reporterResource`, `location`, `lastReceivedOn`, `parameters`, `manifest`, `validateResources`, and output `return`; no `organizationResource`, `measureId`, `measureIdentifier`, `organization`, or `practitioner` parameter is present.
The package defines reporterResource with allowed types rather than as a string parameter.
evidence.quote: "name":"reporterResource" ... "type":"Element" ... "valueUri":"Practitioner" ... "valueUri":"PractitionerRole" ... "valueUri":"Organization"

evidence.detail: The rendered R6 page shows reporterResource as string/reference and adds an organizationResource row.
evidence.quote: reporterResource ... string (reference) ... organizationResource ... 0..1 ... Organization

evidence.detail: R6 examples use undeclared `measureId` and `measureIdentifier` parameters.
evidence.quote: GET [base]/Measure/$collect-data?measureId=measure-mrp ... GET [base]/Measure/$collect-data?measureIdentifier=http://hl7.org/fhir/cqi/ecqm/Measure/Identifier/cms|130

evidence.detail: R6 examples use undeclared `organization` and `practitioner` query parameters.
evidence.quote: organization=Organization/124 ... practitioner=Practitioner/124

evidence.detail: R6 example response still uses the old `measureReport` parameter name.
evidence.quote: "resourceType": "Parameters" ... "name": "measureReport"

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The computable OperationDefinition and rendered operation page can drive different code. Package-driven servers will validate against the package parameter list, while documentation-driven clients or tests can send page-example parameters that are undeclared in the package.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Prefer the package OperationDefinition as the computable contract for generated code and validation. Treat the conflicting R6 examples as suspect until the specification resolves whether the extra names are aliases or stale text. Conformance tests should explicitly assert the intended parameter names rather than copying the rendered examples uncritically.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred goal of the examples is to document common collection scenarios. That goal can be met with a less-breaking and less ambiguous design by aligning examples to the computable R6 parameter names, or by adding intentional alias parameters to the OperationDefinition. The tradeoff is minimal if the examples are stale; if aliases are intended, the specification should bear the explicit alias complexity rather than leaving it implicit.

findings.title: Type-level measure selection no longer accepts the R4 string/reference `measure` parameter

changedFields.oldValue: string
changedFields.newValue: Measure
changedFields.note: R4 modeled `measure` as a string with `searchType: reference`; R6 models it as an inline Measure resource and scopes it to type invocation.

changedFields.oldValue: reference
changedFields.note: The R4 reference-style query parameter is no longer the computable signature for `measure`.
R6 adds a canonical URL selector as an alternative to supplying a Measure resource.
R6 adds a version selector that may only be used with the `url` parameter.

parameterDeltas.name: measure

oldValue.documentation: The measure to evaluate. This parameter is only required when the operation is invoked on the resource type, it is not used when invoking the operation on a Measure instance

newValue.documentation: The measure to evaluate. If the operation is invoked at the instance level, this parameter is not allowed; if the operation is invoked at the type level, this parameter is required, or a url (and optionally version) must be supplied.

parameterDeltas.impactMd: A type-level R4 request or generated wrapper that supplies `measure=Measure/CMS146` as a reference-style string no longer matches the R6 computable input type. For GET invocations, the replacement path is typically the new `url` and optional `version` selector, while POST callers may be able to supply an inline Measure resource.

parameterDeltas.name: url
parameterDeltas.impactMd: This optional R6 selector is additive for R6 clients, but it is not accepted by R4 servers and it replaces the common R4 reference-style selector for type-level invocation.

parameterDeltas.name: version
parameterDeltas.impactMd: Reverse-direction compatibility notes omitted; this report is scoped to R4→R6 compatibility.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same canonical URL, id, operation code `evaluate-measure`, resource `Measure`, and type/instance invocation flags. The changed selector is therefore a contract change within the matched operation, not a replacement operation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The practical break is concentrated on type-level invocation. R4 clients that invoked `[base]/Measure/$evaluate-measure?measure=Measure/CMS146&periodStart=...&periodEnd=...` can fail against an R6 server or R6-generated operation wrapper because `measure` is no longer a string/reference parameter. R6 clients using `url`, `version`, or an inline Measure resource cannot be represented as a plain R4 operation call without a server-specific lookup or transformation. The R6 goal is reasonable: canonical/version selection and inline Measure submission are useful. A less-breaking base design was available, though, by retaining the old reference-style selector as a deprecated alias while adding the new canonical and inline-resource selectors.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Measure-evaluate-measure` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 2. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A quality-reporting client generated from the R4 OperationDefinition calls the type-level endpoint with `measure=Measure/CMS146`. After regenerating against R6, the `measure` parameter is an inline Measure resource, so the old query-style request is rejected or ignored unless the server provides a legacy alias.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have retained the R4 `measure` string/reference parameter, scoped it to type-level invocation, and marked it deprecated while adding `url`/`version` for canonical resolution and a differently named `measureResource` or `measureDefinition` parameter for inline Measure content.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: The tradeoff is an extra selector and precedence rules when multiple selectors are supplied. That cost is modest because R6 already has multiple selectors (`measure` or `url`/`version`), and retaining the old wire shape would preserve existing type-level clients.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This is a direct runtime and code-generation break for a plausible R4 operation call, and the R6 goal could have been achieved with a low-cost compatibility alias. The change deserves renewed design review even though the operation is deprecated in R6.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `measure` as an optional input string with `searchType: reference`.
evidence.quote: {"name":"measure","use":"in","min":0,"max":"1","documentation":"The measure to evaluate. This parameter is only required when the operation is invoked on the resource type, it is not used when invoking the operation on a Measure instance","type":"string","searchType":"reference"}

evidence.detail: R6 changes `measure` to a type-scoped Measure resource and adds type-scoped `url` and `version` selectors.
evidence.quote: measure: type Measure, scope type; url: canonical targetProfile Measure; version: string

evidence.detail: The R4 operation page renders `measure` as `string (reference)`.
evidence.quote: measure ... 0..1 ... string (reference) ... only required when the operation is invoked on the resource type

evidence.detail: The R6 operation page renders `measure` as `Measure`, then adds `url` canonical(Measure) and `version` string.
evidence.quote: measure ... type ... Measure ... url ... type ... canonical(Measure) ... version ... type ... string

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: FHIR operation invocation validates or dispatches named Parameters against the OperationDefinition signature. A generated R6 client/server wrapper will not treat `measure` as a primitive reference query parameter, so an R4-style type-level call can fail validation before measure evaluation starts.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Prefer instance invocation when the Measure resource is already hosted as `[base]/Measure/[id]/$evaluate-measure`. For type-level invocation in R6, use `url` and optional `version` for canonical resolution, or POST a Parameters resource with an inline `Measure` resource if the server supports that form. Servers that need R4 compatibility should accept `measure` as a deprecated reference alias and document selector precedence.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 goal of canonical/version-aware and inline Measure selection is reasonable. It did not require changing the existing `measure` wire parameter from reference-style string to resource type; R6 could have added new selectors while retaining the old selector as a deprecated alias. That less-breaking design would carry modest precedence and documentation cost, but it would preserve most R4 type-level clients.

findings.title: reportType changes from unbound legacy prose codes to a required R6 evaluation-type binding

changedFields.note: R4 had no computable binding on the operation input; R6 requires a specific ValueSet.

changedFields.oldValue: The type of measure report: subject, subject-list, or population. If not specified, a default value of subject will be used if the subject parameter is supplied, otherwise, population will be used
changedFields.newValue: The type of measure report: individual, subject-list, or summary. If not specified, a default value of subject will be used if the subject parameter is supplied and is not a Group, otherwise, summary will be used. NOTE: Implementations should support the use of `subject` for individual and `population` for summary for backwards compatibility with existing implementations.
changedFields.note: The prose changes the primary code names and defaulting semantics while recommending support for two legacy names.

parameterDeltas.name: reportType

newValue.legacyCompatibilityNote: Implementations should support `subject` for individual and `population` for summary.

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 callers using the operation-documented `subject` or `population` values can fail R6 required-binding validation even though the R6 prose asks implementations to support those values for compatibility. Generated R6 clients may expose only the bound R6 codes, while R4 servers may only understand the legacy prose codes.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The reportType parameter exists in both versions with the same name, use, cardinality, and primitive type. The material change is the addition of a required binding and changed code/default prose inside the matched operation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 operation prose explicitly names `subject` and `population`, while R6's required binding is to a ValueSet based on `measure-report-type` codes such as `individual`, `subject-list`, `summary`, and `other` excluding `data-exchange`. A strict R6 validator or generated enum can reject legacy request parameters, and an R6 request using `individual` or `summary` may not be accepted by an R4 server that implemented only the operation's R4 prose. The R6 goal is reasonable because it aligns operation input with the MeasureReport type terminology, but the computable required binding conflicts with the same paragraph's compatibility note unless legacy aliases are also recognized.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Measure-evaluate-measure` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 2. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A conformance test suite sends `reportType=population` because that is one of the R4 operation-documented values. An R6 validator generated from the required binding rejects the parameter before invoking measure calculation, despite the R6 narrative saying implementations should support `population` for compatibility.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have included legacy `subject` and `population` aliases in the required evaluation-type ValueSet as deprecated concepts, or used a weaker operation-level binding for one release while adding an invariant or prose that maps legacy values to `individual` and `summary`.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: Including aliases adds terminology cleanup burden and can perpetuate duplicate names, but it directly implements the R6 compatibility note and avoids validator/client disagreement. A weaker binding would reduce computable strictness but preserve the transition path.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The R6 terminology cleanup is sensible, but the base design makes common R4-documented values computably invalid while simultaneously recommending runtime support for them. That avoidable mismatch deserves review.

evidence.detail: R4 defines reportType as optional code with no binding and prose values `subject`, `subject-list`, and `population`.
evidence.quote: {"name":"reportType","use":"in","min":0,"max":"1","documentation":"The type of measure report: subject, subject-list, or population. If not specified, a default value of subject will be used if the subject parameter is supplied, otherwise, population will be used","type":"code"}

evidence.detail: R6 adds a required binding and changes the primary documented values to `individual`, `subject-list`, and `summary` with a legacy support note.
evidence.quote: "binding":{"strength":"required","valueSet":"http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/measure-report-evaluation-type|6.0.0-ballot4"}

evidence.detail: The required ValueSet includes all `measure-report-type` codes except `data-exchange`; the backing R6 CodeSystem has `individual`, `subject-list`, `summary`, `data-exchange`, and `other`.
evidence.quote: "compose":{"include":[{"system":"http://hl7.org/fhir/measure-report-type"}],"exclude":[{"system":"http://hl7.org/fhir/measure-report-type","concept":[{"code":"data-exchange"}]}]}

evidence.detail: The R6 operation page renders the required binding and the backwards-compatibility note.
evidence.quote: reportType ... code ... Measure Report Evaluation Type (Required) ... individual, subject-list, or summary ... Implementations should support ... subject ... population ... backwards compatibility

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The change affects both runtime request validation and generated operation APIs. Required bindings often become closed enums or validator checks, so legacy R4 request values can be rejected even when the server's measure-evaluation logic could otherwise map them.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Prefer R6 `individual` instead of `subject` and `summary` instead of `population`; keep `subject-list` unchanged. R6 servers should accept and normalize `subject` and `population` if they intend R4 compatibility, and validators should avoid treating the compatibility aliases as fatal errors unless local policy requires strict R6-only inputs.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 goal of aligning `reportType` with MeasureReport terminology is reasonable, but a less-breaking base design could have made the compatibility aliases computable through deprecated ValueSet concepts or a transitional weaker binding. The current design leaves a gap between narrative compatibility and required-binding validation.

findings.title: The practitioner filter is removed and replaced by broader provider/location filters

changedFields.note: R4's practitioner-specific filter is absent from the R6 OperationDefinition.
R6 adds a broader provider filter for Practitioner, PractitionerRole, or Organization references.
R6 adds an optional location filter.

parameterDeltas.name: practitioner

oldValue.documentation: Practitioner for which the measure will be calculated. If specified, the measure will be calculated only for subjects that have a primary relationship to the identified practitioner

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 callers filtering a measure calculation by `practitioner` no longer match the R6 operation signature unless the server implements a legacy alias.

parameterDeltas.name: provider

newValue.documentation: The provider for which the report will be run. This may be a reference to a Practitioner, PractitionerRole, or Organization.

parameterDeltas.impactMd: The R6 replacement is broader and more semantically flexible, but it changes the parameter name that clients, servers, tests, and generated methods use.

parameterDeltas.name: location
parameterDeltas.impactMd: The added `location` parameter is optional and not itself a forward break, but R6 calls using it have no R4 operation equivalent.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The filter change occurs inside the same canonical operation and affects optional input parameters used to constrain subject selection for measure calculation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The break is a named-parameter API break. Existing R4 clients and tests that send `practitioner=Practitioner/123` can fail R6 operation validation or be ignored by servers that only implement `provider`. The R6 goal of broader provider/location attribution is reasonable, but accepting `practitioner` as a legacy alias for Practitioner references would have preserved common R4 calls.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Measure-evaluate-measure` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 2. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A payer or quality registry client evaluates a measure for a clinician panel with `practitioner=Practitioner/abc`. After moving to an R6-generated SDK, the method exposes `provider` instead, and the old request either fails validation or silently returns an unconstrained population if the server ignores unknown parameters.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have retained optional `practitioner` as a deprecated alias limited to Practitioner references while adding `provider` and `location` for broader attribution.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: The main tradeoff is duplicate filter names and precedence rules if both `practitioner` and `provider` are supplied. That burden is modest and can be handled by declaring them mutually exclusive or by making `practitioner` normalize to `provider`.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This appears to be an avoidable API naming break. The broader R6 filter design is useful, but keeping the old parameter as a legacy alias would preserve existing clients with little base-spec cost.

evidence.detail: R4 defines an optional practitioner reference-style string parameter.
evidence.quote: {"name":"practitioner","use":"in","min":0,"max":"1","documentation":"Practitioner for which the measure will be calculated. If specified, the measure will be calculated only for subjects that have a primary relationship to the identified practitioner","type":"string","searchType":"reference"}

evidence.detail: R6 has no `practitioner` parameter and instead defines optional `provider` and `location` reference-style string parameters.
evidence.quote: provider: string reference; location: string reference

evidence.detail: The R4 operation page lists `practitioner` as an input parameter.
evidence.quote: practitioner ... 0..1 ... string (reference) ... primary relationship to the identified practitioner

evidence.detail: The R6 operation page lists `provider` and `location`, with provider allowing Practitioner, PractitionerRole, or Organization.
evidence.quote: provider ... reference to a Practitioner, PractitionerRole, or Organization ... location ... The location for which the report will be run

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: Operation parameters are addressed by name. A server generated from the R6 OperationDefinition is not required to bind the R4 `practitioner` input, and a generated R6 client will expose `provider` instead of `practitioner`.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `practitioner` to `provider` when the R4 value is a Practitioner reference. Do not mechanically map R6 Organization, PractitionerRole, or Location filters back to R4 without policy decisions. Servers supporting R4 clients should accept `practitioner` as an alias and reject requests that supply both alias and replacement with conflicting values.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 goal of broadening the attribution filter is reasonable, but it could have been met by adding `provider` and `location` while retaining `practitioner` as a deprecated alias. That alternative would preserve R4 clients at the cost of a small amount of duplicate parameter handling.

findings.title: The operation result changes from one direct MeasureReport to repeated Bundle returns in a Parameters envelope

changedFields.oldValue: MeasureReport
changedFields.newValue: Bundle
changedFields.note: R4 returns the MeasureReport directly; R6 returns Bundle resources whose first entry is a MeasureReport.
The R6 result can contain zero or more return bundles, so the R4 direct-return shortcut for a sole `return` resource no longer applies.

changedFields.oldValue: Direct MeasureReport resource
changedFields.newValue: Parameters resource with repeated return resources of type Bundle
changedFields.note: The R6 operation page examples show the HTTP response body as `Parameters` with `parameter.name=return` and `parameter.resource=Bundle`.

parameterDeltas.name: return

oldValue.documentation: The results of the measure calculation. See the MeasureReport resource for a complete description of the output of this operation.

newValue.documentation: The result of this operation will be a Bundle for each input subject, where the first entry of the Bundle is a MeasureReport representing the results of the calculation, and subsequent entries in the Bundle are resources created and/or evaluated as part of the calculation.

parameterDeltas.impactMd: Clients that deserialize the HTTP response as a MeasureReport fail against the R6 response shape. R6 results with multiple per-subject bundles or additional evaluated resources cannot be faithfully represented by the R4 single MeasureReport output.

parameterDeltas.name: return
parameterDeltas.impactMd: The output can now be absent or repeated. That changes generated method return types from a single MeasureReport to a collection of Bundles carried in Parameters.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 operation identities and invocation URLs are the same; the finding covers the changed output parameter of the matched operation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Any client that actually consumes `$evaluate-measure` results is likely to notice this change: the R4 page says the sole `return` resource is returned directly as a MeasureReport, while the R6 output is a Parameters envelope containing one or more Bundle resources. Generated SDKs, validators, conformance tests, and polling logic must all change their expected payload shape. The R6 goal is coherent because a Bundle can carry both the MeasureReport and evaluated or created resources, and repeated bundles can represent individual/subject-list results. A less-breaking design is only partial because preserving the direct MeasureReport result would not fully carry the new per-subject and supporting-resource payload without an additional mode or operation.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Measure-evaluate-measure` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 2. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A client polls `$evaluate-measure` and deserializes `HTTP 200` as a MeasureReport. Against an R6 server it receives a Parameters resource with a Bundle in `parameter.resource`; the deserializer fails or the client never finds `MeasureReport.status` for pending/complete handling.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have retained the R4 direct `return: MeasureReport 1..1` for summary and single-subject responses, adding an optional input such as `includeEvaluatedResources` or a separate output/operation for Bundle-returning detailed results.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: That would preserve common R4 clients but create conditional output modes, duplicate result contracts, and more complex rules for subject-list and multi-subject evaluations. It would not fully meet the R6 goal of consistently returning the MeasureReport together with evaluated or created resources for each subject.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The break is large, but the R6 result model addresses real payload needs that a single MeasureReport cannot express cleanly. Because less-breaking alternatives impose meaningful mode and duplication costs, the change appears proportionate even though migration work is substantial.

evidence.detail: R4 defines a required single MeasureReport output.
evidence.quote: {"name":"return","use":"out","min":1,"max":"1","documentation":"The results of the measure calculation. See the MeasureReport resource for a complete description of the output of this operation...","type":"MeasureReport"}

evidence.detail: R6 defines an optional repeatable Bundle output whose first entry is a MeasureReport.
evidence.quote: {"name":"return","use":"out","min":0,"max":"*","documentation":"The result of this operation will be a Bundle for each input subject, where the first entry of the Bundle is a MeasureReport...","type":"Bundle"}

evidence.detail: The R4 operation page states the output is a single MeasureReport and notes direct resource return.
evidence.quote: return ... 1..1 ... MeasureReport ... Note: as this is the only out parameter, it is a resource, and it has the name 'return', the result of this operation is returned directly as a resource

evidence.detail: The R6 operation page states the output is `return` 0..* Bundle and describes the MeasureReport as the first bundle entry.
evidence.quote: return ... 0..* ... Bundle ... first entry of the Bundle is a MeasureReport ... subsequent entries ... resources created and/or evaluated

evidence.detail: The R6 example response starts with Parameters, then a `return` parameter whose resource is a Bundle containing a MeasureReport.
evidence.quote: HTTP/1.1 200 OK ... <Parameters ...><parameter><name value="return"/><resource><Bundle>...<MeasureReport>

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The output wire resource and generated method type both change. The R4 direct-return shortcut applies when the sole output parameter is `return` with max 1; R6 changes max to `*`, so the response is represented as Parameters with repeated Bundle resources rather than a direct MeasureReport.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update clients to parse a Parameters response, iterate all `return` parameters, read each Bundle, and extract the MeasureReport from the first Bundle entry. Treat later Bundle entries as evaluated or created resources.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A less-breaking design could have retained direct MeasureReport output for common summary or single-subject cases and added an opt-in Bundle mode. That would reduce breakage but would also create two output contracts and fail to uniformly represent multi-subject result bundles plus supporting resources. The R6 design is therefore a substantial but understandable break rather than an obviously avoidable rename-style change.

findings.title: R6 removes the Measure instance-level $submit-data endpoint

changedFields.note: R4 permits `[base]/Measure/[id]/$submit-data`; R6 disables instance-level invocation.
The R6 narrative also says the operation is purposefully not allowed on a Measure instance, although the R6 example still shows the old instance URL.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same canonical URL `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/Measure-submit-data`, resource context `Measure`, and wire code `submit-data`; the fanout manifest matched them by canonical URL.

impact.impactRationaleMd: An R4 client following the R4 page or example can invoke `POST [base]/Measure/[id]/$submit-data`. A conformant R6 server generated from `instance: false` need not route that endpoint and may reject it with not-found or operation-not-supported. Server route tables, client SDK methods, and conformance tests that assert instance-level operation support therefore break even before payload parameters are considered.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Measure-submit-data` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 2. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A quality-reporting client built from the R4 example posts CMS146 data to `/Measure/Measure-mrp/$submit-data`; after a server upgrades its base conformance to R6, the generated route no longer exists because only `/Measure/$submit-data` is advertised.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have kept `instance: true` as a deprecated compatibility form for single-measure submissions while recommending the type-level endpoint for multi-measure or multi-subject submissions. The instance form could require the submitted MeasureReport measure reference to match the URL id or warn when it does not.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: This would preserve the common R4 route, but it adds a duplicate endpoint and body/path consistency rules. It also only covers single-measure compatibility; the R6 goal of one request covering multiple measures is naturally served by the type-level route.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The R6 goal is understandable because the MeasureReport body identifies the measure and the operation is being deprecated toward Bundle posting. Still, the old route was explicitly documented and used in examples, and a deprecated compatibility route would be a modest base-design compromise. This deserves renewed review.

evidence.detail: R4 computable definition sets type-level and instance-level invocation.
evidence.quote: "resource":["Measure"],"system":false,"type":true,"instance":true

evidence.detail: R4 operation page lists both type and instance URLs.
evidence.quote: URL: [base]/Measure/$submit-data ... URL: [base]/Measure/[id]/$submit-data

evidence.detail: R6 computable definition disables instance-level invocation.
evidence.quote: "resource":["Measure"],"system":false,"type":true,"instance":false

evidence.detail: R6 narrative explains the removal and lists only the type URL.
evidence.quote: This operation is purposefully not allowed on a Measure instance because the MeasureReport included in the Bundle specifies the measure. ... URL: [base]/Measure/$submit-data

evidence.detail: The R6 example still uses the R4 instance URL, reinforcing migration ambiguity.
evidence.quote: POST [base]/Measure/Measure-mrp/$submit-data

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The route disappears from the formal R6 operation contract. Generated clients lose an instance method, generated servers may not install an instance route, and validators checking CapabilityStatement/OperationDefinition conformance can fail tests that require instance-level support.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Change clients to call `POST [base]/Measure/$submit-data` or, preferably when following the R6 deprecation note, post collection or transaction Bundles to the server root. Compatibility servers can keep accepting the old instance URL and internally dispatch it to the type-level handler after validating or ignoring the URL Measure id according to local policy.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal is reasonable: when the submitted MeasureReport identifies the measure, an instance URL can be redundant and can conflict with multi-measure submissions. A less-breaking base design was nevertheless plausible for the single-measure R4 workflow: keep the instance endpoint as deprecated and define body/path consistency behavior. The tradeoff is duplicate routing and an extra validation branch, not a fundamental incompatibility with the R6 model.

findings.title: R6 replaces flat measureReport/resource inputs with a required repeating bundle input

changedFields.note: The R6 narrative intends submitted Bundles, but the computable type is `MeasureReport`; that inconsistency is reported separately.

changedFields.oldValue: The submit-data operation is used to submit data-of-interest for a measure.
changedFields.newValue: The submit-data operation is used to submit data-of-interest for one or more measures for one or more subjects.
changedFields.note: The operation's scope expands from a single measure-oriented flat payload to grouped per-subject submissions.

parameterDeltas.name: measureReport

oldValue.documentation: The measure report being submitted

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 request bodies that provide the required `measureReport` parameter no longer satisfy the R6 signature because that parameter name is absent.

parameterDeltas.name: resource

oldValue.documentation: The individual resources that make up the data-of-interest being submitted

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R4 request bodies that repeat `resource` for Patient, Encounter, Procedure, or other data-of-interest entries no longer match the R6 parameter contract.

parameterDeltas.name: bundle

newValue.documentation: Bundles for each subject, containing a MeasureReport resource for each Measure being submitted, followed by entries for the data-of-interest for that subject.

parameterDeltas.impactMd: R6 requires at least one `bundle` parameter, repeatable for multiple subjects or groups. Existing flat R4 payloads must be wrapped and regrouped before they are conformant.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same canonical URL `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/Measure-submit-data`, resource context `Measure`, and wire code `submit-data`; the fanout manifest matched them by canonical URL.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The input `Parameters` resource is not backward compatible. An R4-valid operation request with `measureReport` and repeated `resource` parameters is missing the R6-required `bundle` parameter and uses parameter names no longer defined by the operation. Conversely, an R6 request with repeated per-subject Bundles is not directly accepted by an R4 server and may be lossy to flatten if a Bundle contains multiple MeasureReports, transaction metadata, or subject grouping semantics.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Measure-submit-data` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 2. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A measure-reporting submitter creates a Parameters body with one `measureReport` and several `resource` entries, as in R4. An R6 validator or generated server stub rejects it because `bundle` is required and the old parameter names are undefined.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have added repeatable `bundle` as the preferred parameter while retaining `measureReport` and `resource` as deprecated legacy inputs, or defined an explicit alternative input shape for single-subject submissions.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: That would preserve many R4 requests, but it leaves two parallel submission models. Servers would need precedence and conflict rules when both shapes are supplied, and the old flat shape cannot cleanly express multi-subject grouping or transaction/collection Bundle semantics.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The replacement is a real break, but the R6 goal is coherent: grouped Bundles are a better fit for multiple subjects, multiple measures, root Bundle posting, and incremental/snapshot guidance. Because the compatibility alternative has material duplicate-shape and ambiguity costs, the break is probably proportionate apart from the separate R6 type mismatch.

evidence.detail: R4 defines two input parameters.
evidence.quote: "name":"measureReport","use":"in","min":1,"max":"1" ... "name":"resource","use":"in","min":0,"max":"*"

evidence.detail: R4 narrative parameter table documents the flat input shape.
evidence.quote: measureReport 1..1 MeasureReport ... resource 0..* Resource

evidence.detail: R6 defines one required, repeating input parameter.
evidence.quote: "name":"bundle","use":"in","min":1,"max":"*"

evidence.detail: R6 narrative expands the operation to one or more measures/subjects and documents the new bundle parameter.
evidence.quote: one or more measures for one or more subjects ... Each submitted Bundle SHOULD contain resources for a single subject ... bundle 1..*

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: Operation validators and generated server stubs generally dispatch and validate operation requests by `Parameters.parameter.name`, requiredness, repeatability, and resource type. The R6 signature requires `bundle` and removes the R4 names, so old request bodies fail validation or are ignored unless a server implements custom compatibility handling.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Transform each R4 submission into one or more per-subject Bundles. Put the MeasureReport resource for each submitted measure in the Bundle along with the data-of-interest resources, then pass each Bundle as a `bundle` parameter or follow the R6 deprecation note and POST the Bundle to the server root.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A less-breaking R6 base design could have accepted both the old flat parameter set and the new Bundle parameter for a transition. That would preserve most single-measure R4 clients, but it would make the operation harder to validate and document because two shapes represent the same submitted data. The R6 replacement is therefore breaking but reasonably aligned with the multi-subject/multi-measure and root-Bundle-posting direction.

findings.title: R6 names the input `bundle` but formally types it as `MeasureReport` while the narrative/example use Bundle

changedFields.newValue: MeasureReport
changedFields.note: The name, documentation, operation description, and example all indicate that the intended payload resource is `Bundle`, not `MeasureReport`.

changedFields.newValue: Parameters.parameter[name=bundle].resource.resourceType = Bundle
changedFields.note: The R6 example sends a Bundle under the `bundle` parameter, contradicting the formal type shown in both package JSON and rendered parameter table.

parameterDeltas.name: bundle
parameterDeltas.impactMd: An R6 validator or SDK generated from the computable OperationDefinition may require a MeasureReport resource for a parameter named `bundle`, while clients following the operation page will send a Bundle.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same canonical URL `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/Measure-submit-data`, resource context `Measure`, and wire code `submit-data`; the fanout manifest matched them by canonical URL.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The mismatch creates incompatible R6 interpretations. A client migrated from R4 according to the R6 narrative will wrap data in a Bundle and may be rejected by formal OperationDefinition-based validation. A client generated strictly from the package may send a MeasureReport under `bundle`, losing the data-of-interest entries that the narrative says belong in the submitted Bundle.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Measure-submit-data` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 2. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A conformance test uses the R6 example body with `parameter.name = bundle` and `resourceType = Bundle`; an OperationDefinition-driven validator flags it because the formal parameter type is `MeasureReport`.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: If Bundles are intended, set `OperationDefinition.parameter[bundle].type` to `Bundle` and optionally add a profile or documentation describing the required MeasureReport-first/per-subject contents. If MeasureReport is intended, rename the parameter and fix the narrative and example.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: Aligning the computable type with the narrative has little compatibility cost and removes validator/codegen ambiguity. A Bundle profile would add precision without changing the wire shape.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This appears to be an avoidable ballot artifact inconsistency rather than a necessary R6 design break. Because it affects the primary new input parameter and has a low-cost correction, it should be revisited.

evidence.detail: The computable R6 parameter is named `bundle` but typed as `MeasureReport`.
evidence.quote: "name":"bundle","use":"in","min":1,"max":"*","documentation":"Bundles for each subject...","type":"MeasureReport"

evidence.detail: The rendered parameter table repeats the formal `MeasureReport` type while documenting Bundles.
evidence.quote: bundle ... 1..* ... MeasureReport ... Bundles for each subject

evidence.detail: The operation example sends a Bundle under the `bundle` parameter.
evidence.quote: "name": "bundle", "resource": { "resourceType": "Bundle"

evidence.detail: The formal OperationDefinition rendered narrative shows the same mismatch.
evidence.quote: bundle ... 1..* ... MeasureReport ... Bundles for each subject

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The error is in the operation contract used by generators and validators. Tools that build an operation request class from the package may expose a `bundle` argument whose resource type is MeasureReport; tools that validate examples or received requests may reject the Bundle payload that the narrative tells clients to send.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Until the ballot artifact is corrected, implementations should document which interpretation they support. For interoperability, the safer practical interpretation is to accept `Parameters.parameter[name=bundle].resource` with `resourceType: Bundle`, because that matches the parameter name, prose, and example; validators may need a local override for the published OperationDefinition type.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal is per-subject Bundle submission. That goal does not require a breaking or ambiguous formal type: the base OperationDefinition could simply type the parameter as `Bundle` and, if needed, constrain Bundle contents by profile or prose. This would be less breaking for R4 migrations and more reliable for R6 clients than a parameter named `bundle` with type `MeasureReport`.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The candidate is not a canonical URL match, but it is a strong operation-level replacement candidate: both artifacts use code `everything`, title/description `Fetch Product Record`, type and instance invocation, the same `_since` and `_count` input parameters, the same required direct Bundle searchset output, and substantively identical operation narrative. The resource context changes from R4 `MedicinalProduct` to R6 `MedicinalProductDefinition`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: For implementations that support the R4 medicinal product operation, the break is concrete: route tables, generated client methods, conformance tests, and capability-driven discovery keyed to `MedicinalProduct-everything` or `/MedicinalProduct/.../$everything` will not match the R6 base operation. The operation is specialized and R4 FMM 0, so broad ecosystem impact is unlikely, but product regulatory systems that implemented the R4 operation would need an explicit migration. The R6 goal of aligning the operation with the R6 medicinal product definition resource is reasonable; the main compatibility cost is identity/route replacement rather than changed Parameters shape.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `MedicinalProduct-everything` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 0. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A regulatory product registry client generated from R4 discovers `MedicinalProduct-everything` and calls `GET /MedicinalProduct/example/$everything` to retrieve ingredients, packages, authorizations, and linked organizations. Against an R6 server generated from the base package and CapabilityStatement, the advertised operation is `MedicinalProductDefinition-everything`; the old route or canonical lookup fails until the client and tests migrate to `MedicinalProductDefinition`.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have added an explicit deprecated alias or transition OperationDefinition for `MedicinalProduct-everything` that forwarded to `MedicinalProductDefinition-everything`, and the base CapabilityStatement/operations list could have identified it as a legacy-compatible route for one release.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: That would preserve many R4 clients, but it is only a partial operation-level fix because R6 no longer has a base `MedicinalProduct` resource endpoint. Keeping the old route would either imply continued support for a retired resource name or create an operation alias outside the normal resource-scoped model, increasing API surface and migration ambiguity. A fully non-breaking design would depend on the broader resource identity decision, which is outside this operation shard.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This is a real runtime/API break, but the candidate keeps the operation code, invocation levels, parameters, direct Bundle output, and narrative semantics. Given the low maturity of the R4 operation and the close tie to the R6 medicinal product resource replacement, the break appears proportionate even though a clearer transitional alias would have been less disruptive.

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: Runtime break occurs through operation discovery and routing. A client or conformance test that resolves the R4 canonical URL, checks `CapabilityStatement.rest.operation.definition`, or invokes `/MedicinalProduct/$everything` or `/MedicinalProduct/{id}/$everything` will not match the R6 base operation, which is identified and advertised under `MedicinalProductDefinition`. Generated SDKs commonly derive operation methods from the resource name and OperationDefinition id, so method names/routes also change even though the Parameters payload shape does not.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `MedicinalProduct-everything` to `MedicinalProductDefinition-everything` during R6 migration. Update route tables, generated client methods, conformance fixtures, and CapabilityStatement expectations to use `/MedicinalProductDefinition/$everything` and `/MedicinalProductDefinition/{id}/$everything`. Reuse existing `_since`, `_count`, and direct Bundle response handling. If an R6 server needs to support R4 clients during transition, advertise and implement a local compatibility alias deliberately rather than relying on canonical URL matching.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal is reasonable: the operation follows the R6 resource that carries medicinal product definition content while preserving the operation's functional contract. A less-breaking base design was partially available: R6 could have retained a deprecated alias OperationDefinition or explicit legacy route documentation for `MedicinalProduct-everything` while pointing to the new operation. That would reduce route/codegen breakage, but it would also preserve a resource-scoped operation for a resource name absent from R6 base, creating legacy endpoint burden and possible confusion about whether R4 `MedicinalProduct` payload semantics are still supported. Because the operation was R4 trial-use/FMM 0 and the R6 replacement is close in semantics and parameters, the operation-level break is breaking but probably acceptable.

findings.title: Multiple matching identifiers change from mandatory error to preference/date-based resolution

changedFields.oldValue: If there are multiple possible identifiers of the specified type (e.g. multiple OIDs) the server returns an error.
changedFields.newValue: If there is more than one identifier of the specified type (for the specified date), then the 'preferred' identifier will be returned. If there is only one identifier, that identifier will be returned even if it is not preferred. If there are multiple preferred identifiers or multiple identifiers with none marked as preferred, the system MAY return an error or may list all identifiers applicable for that date and period.
changedFields.note: The R6 semantic rule can turn an R4 OperationOutcome/error expectation into a successful result when a single preferred identifier exists.

changedFields.oldValue: Idempotent operation; multiple possible identifiers of the requested type produce an error.
changedFields.newValue: Idempotent operation; multiple identifiers are filtered by date and preference, with remaining ambiguity handled by MAY error or listing applicable identifiers.
changedFields.note: The output parameter remains `result` 1..1 string, so the R6 prose about listing all identifiers is potentially ambiguous for strict output-shape implementations.

parameterDeltas.name: result

oldValue.operationComment: Multiple possible identifiers of the specified type produce an error.

newValue.operationComment: A preferred identifier may be returned among multiple identifiers; unresolved ambiguity MAY produce an error or list applicable identifiers.

parameterDeltas.impactMd: The result parameter's computable shape did not change, but the circumstances under which a success result is returned changed materially.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The same canonical operation is being compared. The changed behavior comes from operation-specific prose/comment text, not from a changed URL, code, resource scope, or input/output cardinality.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is the only direct R4-to-R6 runtime behavior change found for the shard. An R4 conformance test could seed a NamingSystem with multiple OIDs and expect an error, while an R6-conformant server may return the one marked preferred for the requested date. R4 clients that used error responses to detect ambiguous metadata can receive a success response instead. The R6 goal is reasonable because the operation is named `preferred-id` and NamingSystem unique identifiers can carry preference and period metadata. A less-breaking alternative is only partial: R6 could have preserved the R4 error default and introduced preference/date resolution behind an opt-in parameter, but that would complicate the operation and continue a behavior that ignores the preferred identifier.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `NamingSystem-preferred-id` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 1. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A terminology server has a NamingSystem with two OIDs for the same system, one marked preferred during the requested period. An R4 regression test expects `$preferred-id&type=oid` to fail because multiple OIDs exist; an R6 implementation returns the preferred OID with HTTP 200.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have retained the R4 default rule that any multiple identifiers of the requested type produce an error unless a new optional parameter explicitly requested preference/date resolution, or it could have required an error when multiple identifiers exist and no `date` is supplied.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: That would preserve tests relying on ambiguity errors, but it would make the default behavior less useful for an operation named `preferred-id`, require another compatibility switch, and leave clients without a simple default way to obtain the preferred identifier.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The behavior change can break runtime expectations, but it is proportionate: it makes the operation honor preference and period semantics instead of failing in the common reason the operation exists. The partial less-breaking alternative has real complexity and semantic tradeoffs, so this does not rise to `Revisit`.

evidence.detail: R4 requires an error when multiple possible identifiers of the requested type exist.
evidence.quote: If there are multiple possible identifiers of the specified type (e.g. multiple OIDs) the server returns an error.

evidence.detail: R6 returns the preferred identifier among multiple matches for the specified date and allows error or listing only for remaining ambiguous cases.
evidence.quote: If there is more than one identifier of the specified type (for the specified date), then the 'preferred' identifier will be returned.

evidence.detail: The R4 operation page repeats the error-on-multiple rule.
The R6 operation page repeats the preference/date rule and the MAY error/list handling for unresolved ambiguity.

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The same request can now yield a different success/error outcome. R4 behavior was deterministic for multiple possible identifiers: return an error. R6 first narrows by date and preference, so a server can return a `Parameters` response with `result` even when more than one identifier of the requested type exists in the NamingSystem history.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update server logic and conformance tests that assumed all multiple-identifier cases are errors. Tests should cover a single identifier, multiple identifiers with exactly one preferred identifier for the date, multiple preferred identifiers, and multiple identifiers with none preferred. Clients should not rely on an error as the only signal of ambiguity; they should validate whether the returned identifier satisfies the requested type and date policy.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal is to make `$preferred-id` actually resolve the preferred identifier, including historical preference by date. That goal could have been pursued with an opt-in parameter or a legacy error default, but the alternative is only partially less-breaking because it preserves less useful semantics and adds branching to an already small operation. Keeping the R4 behavior unchanged would avoid some regression-test changes but would not meet the R6 goal as directly.

findings.title: $lastn result ordering changed from apparent global recency sorting to code-group-first ordering

changedFields.oldValue: Response is grouped by Observation.code and then says it is sorted from most recent to oldest.
changedFields.newValue: Response is ordered first by equivalent Observation.code; the ordering of equivalent code groups is not specified; within each code group observations are ordered from most recent effective time to oldest effective time.
changedFields.note: The selected observation set and parameter contract are unchanged; the potential compatibility issue is Bundle entry ordering.

changedFields.newValue: R6 adds that individual Observation.code values used for grouping might not be explicit in the request, for example when a category is requested or code:below is used.
changedFields.note: This clarification supports the grouped-selection model but can surprise clients that expected requested codes to directly define output groups.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The shard is a direct canonical-url match: both artifacts use `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/Observation-lastn`, code `lastn`, resource `Observation`, and type-level invocation (`system=false`, `type=true`, `instance=false`).

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 clients or tests that assert the returned Bundle entries are globally newest-to-oldest across all Observation codes may fail against an R6-conformant server that emits entries grouped by code with unspecified group order. The returned resources, operation URL, input parameters, and output resource type remain stable, so the risk is concentrated in order-sensitive UI rendering, paging-like assumptions, validators, and conformance tests rather than generated parameter APIs.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Observation-lastn` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 3. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A vital-signs dashboard calls `GET [base]/Observation/$lastn?patient=123&category=vital-signs&max=1` and renders `Bundle.entry` in server order. Under the R4 reading, its tests expect the latest temperature, blood pressure, and weight observations to be globally descending by effective time; an R6 server may return code groups in an arbitrary order with only within-group recency sorted.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have clarified that grouping determines membership and the per-code `max` limit, while preserving a final Bundle order sorted globally by effective time. Another less-breaking option would be to require a stable code-group sort key instead of leaving group order unspecified.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: A global final sort interleaves code groups and can be less convenient for grouped displays. A stable code-group sort would require additional coding/text collation rules and could imply meaning where none exists. R4's original wording was also ambiguous, so not every implementation or client will experience this as a behavior break.

freshReview.rationaleMd: The R6 goal appears reasonable: make the grouped nature of `$lastn` explicit and avoid over-specifying cross-code order when returned codes may not have been explicit in the request. There is real migration risk for order-sensitive clients and conformance tests, but the core operation contract is stable and less-breaking alternatives have meaningful tradeoffs, so the change is probably acceptable rather than needing renewed design attention.

evidence.detail: R4 operation narrative groups by code and then states a newest-to-oldest sort.
evidence.quote: The response from a lastn query is a set of observations: ... * 'GROUP BY' `Observation.code` ... * Sorted from most recent to the oldest

evidence.detail: R6 operation narrative changes the ordering model to code-group-first and confines recency sorting to within groups.
evidence.quote: * Ordered first by "equivalent" `Observation.code` value ... * The ordering of the "equivalent" code groups is not specified. * Ordered secondly (within each code group) from most recent effective time to the oldest effective time.

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: An R6 server can select the same per-code last-N observations but serialize the Bundle grouped by code, with no specified ordering between code groups. R4 clients that consumed the Bundle as an already globally time-sorted stream may render a different sequence or fail tests, even though the individual returned Observations and the `max` semantics are unchanged.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Treat `$lastn` output as a grouped result set in R6. Clients that need a globally newest-to-oldest presentation should sort returned Observations client-side by `Observation.effective[x]` after applying or trusting the server's per-code `max` selection. Server conformance tests should assert within-code-group recency and per-code max/tie behavior, not cross-code Bundle order.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal is reasonable: clarify grouped output semantics and avoid assigning significance to the order of code groups, especially when grouping codes may be discovered through `category` or `code:below` rather than explicitly listed by the client. A less-breaking base design was partially available: keep a final global recency sort after group selection, or specify a stable group sort. Those alternatives would preserve more R4 order-sensitive behavior, but they add cross-group ordering obligations that may not help grouped consumers and were not unambiguously required by the R4 text.

findings.title: `statistic` input parameter gained a required ValueSet binding

changedFields.note: R4 had no computable OperationDefinition binding on the `statistic` code parameter; R6 binds it required to the observation-statistics ValueSet.

parameterDeltas.name: statistic
parameterDeltas.impactMd: A `$stats` Parameters request containing a local or otherwise out-of-ValueSet `statistic` code could be accepted by R4 tooling that only read the computable OperationDefinition, but is not base-conformant under R6 validation against the OperationDefinition.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The operation is the same canonical operation in both versions: the URL remains `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/Observation-stats`, the wire code remains `$stats`, the resource scope remains `Observation`, and invocation remains type-level (`system=false`, `type=true`, `instance=false`).

impact.impactRationaleMd: The concrete break is strongest for validators, generated operation clients, conformance tests, or servers that enforce OperationDefinition bindings: a previously unbound R4 `valueCode` can become invalid if it is not in the R6 observation-statistics ValueSet. Runtime prevalence appears low because the R4 narrative already directed clients to StatisticsCode and listed the standard statistics, but the absence of a computable R4 binding left room for local codes in generated or validator-driven workflows.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Observation-stats` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 3. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A generated R4 client sends `statistic=local-z-score` to a server that implemented a local extension of `$stats`; an R6 conformance test or server validator using the R6 OperationDefinition rejects that Parameters input because the code is outside the required observation-statistics ValueSet.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have added a preferred or extensible binding instead of a required binding, or added a separate explicitly profiled/custom extension path for local statistics while keeping the base `statistic` parameter open.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: Those designs would preserve more R4-generated local-code traffic, but they weaken the base operation's computable contract and make it harder for clients to know which statistic components a conformant server will return. A required binding is proportionate for a standard operation whose semantics depend on shared statistic code meanings.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This is a real computable conformance tightening, but the R6 goal is reasonable: make the operation's statistic vocabulary machine-checkable and interoperable. Because R4 narrative already pointed to the same statistics vocabulary, custom-code use is likely non-standard and rare; less-breaking alternatives exist but materially reduce validation clarity.

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: Operation validators and servers that use the R6 OperationDefinition can validate each repeated `statistic` input as a code from the required observation-statistics ValueSet. Requests with local code values that were not rejected by R4's unbound computable definition can now fail validation or conformance testing before calculation.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Audit `$stats` callers and tests for `statistic` values outside the standard observation-statistics code set. Replace local statistic names with standard codes where possible. If local statistics are required, document them in an implementation-specific profile or extension rather than assuming they are accepted by the base R6 operation, and test both request validation and returned Observation.component coding behavior.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal is to make a previously narrative-only statistic vocabulary constraint computable. A less-breaking base design could have used a preferred or extensible binding, preserving local R4 traffic, but that would undercut a standard operation whose output semantics depend on shared statistic code meanings. The required binding is therefore breaking for a narrow class of implementations but probably proportionate.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The fanout manifest classifies `Patient-everything` as `r4-only`/`unmatched`. The R4 package file and index contain the canonical `http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/Patient-everything`; the R6 package has no same file or index entry, and the R6 operations registry omits the Patient `$everything` row. R6 rendered pages with the same page names still exist, so this is best characterized as a computable package/registry removal or publication inconsistency rather than a clean semantic replacement.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Patient `$everything` is a common full-record access operation, explicitly tied in R4 to Blue Button and bulk patient-record retrieval. R4 clients, servers, generated SDKs, validators, and test suites that load core OperationDefinitions from the package lose the canonical operation, route metadata, idempotence signal, and parameter definitions in R6. The practical break is strongest for package-driven tooling and conformance, while runtime route support is ambiguous because the R6 rendered pages still document the operation.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Patient-everything` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A server framework regenerates its R6 operation registry from `hl7.fhir.r6.core`; it drops the generated Patient `$everything` handler and its conformance test, while SMART/Blue Button clients still call `/Patient/{id}/$everything` based on prior R4 support and the R6 rendered page.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: Keep `OperationDefinition/Patient-everything` in the R6 core package and operations registry with the same canonical URL, Patient type/instance invocation levels, idempotent behavior, and existing parameter table. If R6 intended to refine safety, paging, version-specific references, or IG-specific minimum content rules, add that as narrative/conformance guidance or deprecation text rather than removing the computable operation.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: Retaining the artifact requires continued maintenance of a broad and potentially expensive full-record operation, and it may keep pressure on servers to support an operation some deployments prefer to constrain. Those tradeoffs are modest compared with breaking package-driven discovery for a mature Patient access workflow, especially because the R6 rendered pages already continue to document the operation.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This deserves renewed standards or publication review because the computable package and operation registry disagree with R6 rendered pages, the operation is mature and practically important, and a low-cost less-breaking design exists: keep the canonical OperationDefinition while refining its narrative requirements.

evidence.quote: The canonical URL for this operation definition is ... http://hl7.org/fhir/OperationDefinition/Patient-everything ... URL: [base]/Patient/$everything ... URL: [base]/Patient/[id]/$everything ... This is an idempotent operation

findings.runtimeMechanismMd: The concrete break is not a changed HTTP parameter value; it is disappearance of the computable operation artifact from `hl7.fhir.r6.core`. Package-driven servers may stop registering `/Patient/$everything` and `/Patient/{id}/$everything`; package-driven clients may lose generated methods or request builders; validators and conformance tests cannot resolve the canonical OperationDefinition or verify the `Parameters` request/response shape. If a server still supports the route based on the R6 rendered page, package-based tooling will nevertheless see it as non-core or locally defined.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Until the R6 publication intent is clarified, R4-to-R6 implementers should treat Patient `$everything` as a special compatibility surface. Servers that support it should advertise it explicitly in their own CapabilityStatement and, if needed, publish a local copy or dependency-pinned copy of the OperationDefinition rather than relying on discovery from `hl7.fhir.r6.core`. Client and test tooling should not silently drop existing Patient `$everything` workflows solely because the R6 package omits the artifact; instead, check server CapabilityStatements and implementation-guide requirements.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The inferred R6 goal is unclear. If the goal was to retire a broad Patient full-record operation because of privacy, performance, or overlap with Group `$everything`/bulk export patterns, that goal is understandable but not clearly achieved by an unannounced package/registry omission while R6 pages still document the operation. A less-breaking base R6 design would have retained the canonical OperationDefinition and routes, added normative safety and paging guidance, or marked the operation deprecated with a replacement path.

findings.title: R6 splits match result controls and changes onlyCertainMatches behavior

oldOperation.name: Find patient matches using MPI based logic

changedFields.note: R6 adds one optional input parameter between `resource` and `onlyCertainMatches`.

newValue.documentation: If there are multiple potential matches, the server should identify the single most appropriate match that should be used with future interactions with the server (for example, as part of a subsequent create interaction).

changedFields.note: This adds an explicit request for a single most appropriate match.

changedFields.oldValue: If there are multiple potential matches, then the match should not return the results with this flag set to true.  When false, the server may return multiple results with each result graded accordingly.
changedFields.newValue: If there are multiple potential matches, the server should be certain that each of the records are for the same patients.  This could happen if the records are duplicates, are the same person for the purpose of data segregation, or other reasons.  When false, the server may return multiple results with each result graded accordingly.
changedFields.note: R6 changes the flag from a 'do not return results when multiple potential matches exist' instruction to a certainty filter that can still allow multiple records when they are considered the same patient.

parameterDeltas.name: onlySingleMatch

newValue.documentation: If there are multiple potential matches, the server should identify the single most appropriate match that should be used with future interactions with the server (for example, as part of a subsequent create interaction).

parameterDeltas.impactMd: Adds an optional R6 request control. R4 clients are not required to send it, but R6 clients that depend on it will not have an equivalent standard parameter on R4 servers, and generated operation helpers will expose a new optional argument.

parameterDeltas.name: onlyCertainMatches
parameterDeltas.oldValue: If there are multiple potential matches, then the match should not return the results with this flag set to true.  When false, the server may return multiple results with each result graded accordingly.
parameterDeltas.newValue: If there are multiple potential matches, the server should be certain that each of the records are for the same patients.  This could happen if the records are duplicates, are the same person for the purpose of data segregation, or other reasons.  When false, the server may return multiple results with each result graded accordingly.
parameterDeltas.impactMd: Changes the practical meaning of an existing optional flag for the same wire request. A server following R6 can return multiple records for `onlyCertainMatches=true` when it considers them duplicates or otherwise the same patient, while the R4 text told servers not to return results in the presence of multiple potential matches.

findings.matchRationaleMd: The R4 and R6 artifacts have the same id, canonical URL, operation code, resource context, and invocation flags. The fanout row classifies them as a common `canonical-url` match, so the parameter/prose delta is a change to the same Patient `$match` operation rather than a replacement operation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The same R4-style request can be interpreted differently by an R6 server: `onlyCertainMatches=true` no longer necessarily suppresses multiple candidate results if the server considers the returned Patient records to be the same person. That can affect registration, duplicate-check, or create-before-link workflows that used the R4 flag to avoid ambiguous automated decisions. The added `onlySingleMatch` parameter gives R6 clients a clearer way to request one usable match, but R4 clients and R4 servers do not know that parameter. The impact is not High because the operation already returns a Bundle, the R4 text used SHOULD-level language and left algorithm details to implementations, and only clients using this optional flag are exposed.

fmmContext.rationaleMd: R4 baseline for `Patient-match` is standards-status `trial-use` and FMM 5. For this R4→R6 analysis, that R4 maturity/status is the stability pressure. R6 maturity/status is not used to increase the burden for breaking R4 clients or servers.

freshReview.realWorldScenarioMd: A registration client posts `Patient/$match` with a partial Patient and `onlyCertainMatches=true` before deciding whether to create a new Patient. Against an R4-style server it expects no returned results when multiple candidates exist; against an R6-style server it may receive several duplicate/same-patient records unless it also knows to request `onlySingleMatch=true`.

lessBreakingAlternative.candidateDesignMd: R6 could have added `onlySingleMatch` while explicitly preserving the R4 interpretation of `onlyCertainMatches=true` when `onlySingleMatch` is absent, and introduced a separate opt-in parameter or conformance note for returning multiple certain duplicate/same-patient records.
lessBreakingAlternative.tradeoffsOrReasonMd: That design would reduce surprise for legacy clients but would keep an awkward R4 flag alive, add another result-control distinction, and make it harder for servers to return clinically useful duplicate/same-person records without a new opt-in. The R6 split is reasonable, but the compatibility burden is high enough that the default behavior and migration note deserve standards review.

freshReview.rationaleMd: This is not a route removal or cardinality/type break, but it is a runtime semantic change to a mature Patient matching operation. The R6 goal of separating 'single best match' from 'only certain matches' is reasonable; however, a lower-break design could have made the new behavior opt-in while preserving legacy `onlyCertainMatches` semantics by default. Because patient identity workflows can make automated create/link decisions, the change warrants renewed review rather than being treated as mere documentation cleanup.
